knowledge_statements.scope_note: Introduces one auxiliary block for each affine-composed objective or inequality term. The nonlinear terms use distinct blocks, although the added affine equalities continue to couple those blocks through the original variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the problem with objective \(f_0(A_0x+b_0)\), inequalities \(f_i(A_ix+b_i)\leq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and equalities \(h_j(x)=0\) for \(j=1,\ldots,p\), where \(A_i\in\mathbf R^{k_i\times n}\), \(b_i\in\mathbf R^{k_i}\), and \(f_i:\mathbf R^{k_i}\to\mathbf R\). Introduce \(y_i\in\mathbf R^{k_i}\) and impose \(y_i=A_ix+b_i\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\). The lifted problem with objective \(f_0(y_0)\), inequalities \(f_i(y_i)\leq0\), the linking equalities, and the original equalities \(h_j(x)=0\) is equivalent to the original problem. Each original feasible \(x\) has exactly one lifted feasible extension \((x,y)\), and optimal points correspond under projection to \(x\). The lift adds \(\sum_{i=0}^m k_i\) scalar variables and the same number of scalar equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine-composed objective and inequality terms can be separated into auxiliary blocks linked to the original variable by affine equalities. The lift preserves feasibility and optimality and adds the same number of scalar variables as scalar linking equations. The nonlinear terms become block-separated, but the linking equations still couple them through the original variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_i=A_ix+b_i\ (i=0,\ldots,m)\) gives a one-to-one feasible extension of each \(x\), preserves optimal \(x\)-points under projection, and adds \(\sum_{i=0}^m k_i\) scalar variables and equalities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A strongly convex smooth specialization of convex minimization with finitely many functional inequalities and a simple set constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a simple closed convex set, and let \(f_i\in\mathcal{S}_{\mu,L}^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\) for \(i=0,1,\ldots,m\), where \(\mu>0\). The constrained minimization problem is
\[
\min_{x\in Q} f_0(x)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
f_i(x)\le 0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a smooth strongly convex objective over a simple closed convex set subject to finitely many smooth strongly convex functional inequalities.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is simple, closed, and convex}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an extended-real composite objective, its minimization problem, conditional minimizer notation, and the diameter of its bounded domain set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a fixed norm, let \(Q\subset\mathbb E\) be nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex, let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable, and let \(\Psi:\mathbb E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex with \(\operatorname{dom}\Psi\subseteq Q\). Extend \(f\) by \(f(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\notin Q\), and define \(\bar f(x)=f(x)+\Psi(x)\). The associated composite convex minimization problem is \(\min_{x\in\mathbb E}\bar f(x)\). A minimizer, if one exists, is denoted by \(x^*\), and \(D=\operatorname{diam}(Q)=\sup\{\|x-y\|:x,y\in Q\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The composite objective is the sum of a differentiable convex term and a proper closed convex extended-real term whose domain lies in a nonempty bounded closed convex set. The first term is extended by positive infinity outside that set. A minimizer is denoted by x* only if one exists, and D denotes the set's diameter in the fixed norm.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space equipped with a fixed norm \(\|\cdot\|\).
\(Q\subset\mathbb E\) is nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex.
\(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) is convex and differentiable and is extended by \(+\infty\) outside \(Q\).
\(\Psi:\mathbb E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, and convex, with \(\operatorname{dom}\Psi\subseteq Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar f=f+\Psi,\qquad \min_{x\in\mathbb E}\bar f(x),\qquad x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb E}\bar f(x)\ \text{when this argmin is nonempty},\qquad D=\sup_{x,y\in Q}\|x-y\|.\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminological problem-class definition. Despite its name, the displayed homogeneous formulation minimizes over a specified closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space. Let \(f:\mathbb E\to\mathbb R\) be convex, satisfy \(f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb E\) and \(\lambda\ge0\), and have \(\operatorname{dom}f=\mathbb E\). Let \(Q_1\subset\mathbb E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex with \(0\notin Q_1\), and assume \(0\in\operatorname{int}\partial f(0)\). The problem \[\min_{x\in Q_1}f(x),\qquad f^*:=\min_{x\in Q_1}f(x),\] together with these assumptions is called a conic unconstrained minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic unconstrained minimization problem minimizes an everywhere-finite convex objective that is positively homogeneous of degree one over a nonempty closed convex set not containing the origin, under the condition that zero lies in the interior of the objective's subdifferential at zero.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb E\text{ is a finite-dimensional real vector space}
\varnothing\ne Q_1\subset\mathbb E\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in Q_1}f(x)\text{ with these data is a conic unconstrained minimization problem}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth convex minimization over a closed convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A constrained convex model with a globally Lipschitz gradient measured in a specified primal-dual ellipsoidal norm pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be positive definite, with \(\|x\|_G=\sqrt{\langle Gx,x\rangle}\) and \(\|s\|_G^*=\sqrt{\langle G^{-1}s,s\rangle}\). Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Let \(\phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable, and suppose that for some \(L>0\),
\[
\|\nabla\phi(x)-\nabla\phi(y)\|_G^*\le L\|x-y\|_G\qquad\forall x,y\in\mathbb R^n.
\]
The associated smooth constrained convex minimization problem is
\[
\min\{\phi(x):x\in Q\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth constrained convex minimization problem minimizes a differentiable convex function over a nonempty closed convex set, assuming that the function's gradient is globally Lipschitz in the specified primal-dual G-norm pair.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
\phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex and differentiable}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composite Convex Minimization Model with a Tractable Proximal Subproblem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies a smooth-plus-closed-convex problem class together with the prox geometry and auxiliary optimization access assumed by the associated first-order method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq E\) be closed and convex. Let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable with \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|^*\le L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in Q\), and let \(\Psi:Q\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be closed and convex. The composite problem is \(\min_{x\in Q}\tilde f(x)\), where \(\tilde f(x)=f(x)+\Psi(x)\). Let \(d:Q\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(1\)-strongly convex on \(Q\). Assume that for every \(s\in E^*\) and every \(\alpha,\beta\ge0\), \(\min_{x\in Q}\{\langle s,x\rangle+\alpha d(x)+\beta\Psi(x)\}\) is tractable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model minimizes the sum of a convex smooth function with Lipschitz-continuous gradient and a closed convex extended-valued function over a closed convex set. Its access assumptions include a differentiable strongly convex prox-function and tractability of every specified linear-prox-composite auxiliary problem.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq E\text{ is closed and convex}
f:Q\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex and differentiable}
d:Q\to\mathbb R\text{ is differentiable and }1\text{-strongly convex on }Q
\min_{x\in Q}\{\langle s,x\rangle+\alpha d(x)+\beta\Psi(x)\}\text{ is tractable for all }s\in E^*,\ \alpha,\beta\ge0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal Accessibility Does Not Ensure Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence boundary for the smooth-plus-proximable architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), let \(f(x)=0\) and \(g(x)=e^x\). For every \(\gamma>0\) and \(z\in\mathbb R\), \[\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(z)=z-W(\gamma e^z),\] where \(W\) is the principal Lambert function, so the proximal point is uniquely defined and explicitly evaluable. Nevertheless, \(\inf_x(f(x)+g(x))=0\) and the infimum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separated gradient and proximal access alone do not guarantee existence of a composite minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Accessibility Does Not Ensure Attainment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convexity of the Composite Objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic structural consequence of the smooth finite-valued component and the proper closed convex proximal component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable, and let \(g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex. Then \(F=f+g\) is proper, closed, and convex, with \(\operatorname{dom}F=\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a finite smooth convex function to a proper closed convex proximable term preserves properness, closedness, convexity, and its effective domain.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is convex and differentiable.
\(g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F=f+g\text{ is proper, closed, and convex, and }\operatorname{dom}F=\operatorname{dom}g.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convexity of the Composite Objective
Smooth-Plus-Proximable Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional convex composite model with gradient and proximal access separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\). A smooth-plus-proximable model is the problem \[\min_{x\in X} F(x):=f(x)+g(x),\] where \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient for some \(L>0\), and \(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex. The component \(g\) is called proximable when, for every \(z\in X\) and relevant \(\gamma>0\), the uniquely defined point \[\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(z):=\arg\min_{x\in X}\left\{g(x)+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\lVert x-z\rVert^2\right\}\] is available through an exact or specified-accuracy oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is a smooth convex term with Lipschitz gradient plus a closed convex term whose proximal subproblem is computationally accessible.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, closed, convex, and proximally accessible
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=f+g\) has separated gradient and proximal oracle structure.

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of the nonsmooth component

children.title: Multiple Nonsmooth Component Models
children.top_down_role: Additive models requiring several nonsmooth components to remain independently accessible.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order characterization for a finite sum of convex components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the proper closed convex functions \(g_i\) satisfy \(\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_i)\ne\varnothing\), then \[\partial\Big(\sum_{i=1}^m g_i\Big)(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\partial g_i(x).\] Consequently, \(x^\star\) minimizes the sum exactly when there exist \(v_i\in\partial g_i(x^\star)\) with \(\sum_i v_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the standard relative-interior qualification, balancing one subgradient from each component exactly certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) is proper, closed, and convex
knowledge_statements.title: Qualified Finite-Sum Rule and Optimality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal Maps of Components Do Not Generally Compose
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary motivating splitting formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In general, \(\operatorname{prox}_{g_1+g_2}\ne\operatorname{prox}_{g_1}\circ\operatorname{prox}_{g_2}\). Let \(g_1=\delta_U\) and \(g_2=\delta_V\) on \(\mathbb R^2\), where \(U=\{(t,0):t\in\mathbb R\}\) and \(V=\{(t,t):t\in\mathbb R\}\). The component proximal maps are the orthogonal projections onto \(U\) and \(V\); their composition is not the projection onto \(U\cap V=\{0\}\), whereas \(\operatorname{prox}_{g_1+g_2}\) is the constant zero map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate proximal maps ordinarily cannot be composed to obtain the proximal map of the sum.
assumptions_latex: Proximal maps use the Euclidean metric
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Maps of Components Do Not Generally Compose

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite additive convex model retaining separately specified access to each component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge2\). A multiple nonsmooth component model has objective \[F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x),\] where the \(g_i\) are proper closed convex functions with a common domain point and are retained as separately accessible components through specified primitives such as values, subgradients, or proximal mappings. The definition does not assume that \(\operatorname{prox}_F\) is directly available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is a sum of at least two separately accessible closed convex components, without assuming a proximal oracle for their sum.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) is proper, closed, and convex
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F=\sum_{i=1}^mg_i\text{ is a proper convex objective with separately retained component structure}.

notation.meaning: component i of the finite nonsmooth sum

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Nonsmooth Component Model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lift retaining separate component objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x)\), \[\inf_xF(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x_i):x_i=z\ \text{for all }i\right\}.\] Finite minimizers correspond through \(x_i=z=x^\star\). The lift separates the component objectives and places their coupling in consensus equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One copy of the decision per component plus consensus constraints gives an exact separated formulation.
assumptions_latex: The finite sum is interpreted in the extended-real sense
knowledge_statements.title: Consensus-Lift Representation
Multiple Nonsmooth Component Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive convex model retaining separate oracle access to each nonsmooth component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) and let \(m\geq 2\). A multiple nonsmooth component model has the form \[\min_{x\in X} F(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m} g_i(x),\] where every \(g_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{dom}g_i\neq\varnothing\). The components remain independently accessible: an oracle accepts an index \(i\) and returns a prescribed primitive for \(g_i\), such as a value, a subgradient at a domain point, or a proximal point. No assumption is made that the proximal mapping of the full sum is directly available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is a sum of at least two closed convex nonsmooth terms, each accessed separately rather than through a proximal oracle for the whole sum.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i\) is proper, closed, and convex for every \(i\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\sum_{i=1}^{m}g_i\) is a proper convex objective with component-indexed access.

children.title: Loss-Plus-Regularizer Models
children.top_down_role: Models separating data fidelity from structural preference.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order condition for the positive-weight model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\lambda>0\), \(\mathcal L\) and \(R\) are proper convex, and \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}\mathcal L)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}R)\ne\varnothing\), then \[x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}(\mathcal L+\lambda R)\iff0\in\partial\mathcal L(x^\star)+\lambda\partial R(x^\star).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-interior qualification makes the summed loss and regularizer subgradients an exact optimality test.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualified Loss-Regularizer Optimality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex objective architecture separating data fidelity from structural preference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed data set \(D\) and \(\lambda>0\), a loss-plus-regularizer model minimizes \[F_D(x)=\mathcal L(x;D)+\lambda R(x),\] where \(\mathcal L(\cdot;D)\) is a proper convex data-fidelity loss and \(R\) is a proper convex structural penalty. If their domains intersect, \(F_D\) is proper convex. When regularization is to be disabled, the zero-weight model is defined separately as \(F_{D,0}=\mathcal L(\cdot;D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive multiple of a convex structural penalty is added to a convex data-fitting loss; the unregularized case is defined separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_D=\mathcal L(\cdot;D)+\lambda R\text{ is proper convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss-Plus-Regularizer Model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for disabling an extended-valued regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(R\) can equal \(+\infty\), the expression \(\mathcal L+0R\) is convention-dependent. Defining the unregularized model as \(F_0=\mathcal L\) removes every effect of \(R\). Under the alternative convention \(0\cdot(+\infty)=+\infty\), one instead obtains \(F_0=\mathcal L+\delta_{\operatorname{dom}R}\), so the domain restriction remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero weight may either remove an extended-valued regularizer or retain its domain as a hard constraint, so the intended convention must be explicit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_0=\mathcal L\text{ must be defined separately when zero weight is intended to remove all effects of }R.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Weight Extended-Value Convention
Loss-Plus-Regularizer Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex objective architecture separating data fidelity from structural regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(D\) denote fixed observed data, and let \(\lambda\geq 0\). A loss-plus-regularizer model is \[\min_{x\in X} F_D(x):=\mathcal{L}(x;D)+\lambda R(x),\] where \(\mathcal{L}(\cdot;D):X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper convex data-fidelity function and \(R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper convex penalty encoding structural preference. The model is well posed as a proper convex objective whenever \(\operatorname{dom}\mathcal{L}(\cdot;D)\cap\operatorname{dom}R\neq\varnothing\); smoothness or proximal accessibility is an additional, not defining, property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex data-fitting loss is combined with a nonnegative multiple of a convex structural penalty, with compatible effective domains.

review_flags: The cited affine-convexity locator requires full-text confirmation for the composite-function formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex outer function composed with an affine map, optionally plus a direct convex term.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Affine Sets and Convex Sets p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y=\mathbb{R}^p\), let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(b\in Y\). An affine-composite objective admits the representation \[F(x)=h(Ax+b)+g(x),\] where \(h:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions. If there exists \(x\in\operatorname{dom}g\) such that \(Ax+b\in\operatorname{dom}h\), then \(F\) is proper and convex on \(X\). No monotonicity hypothesis on \(h\) is needed because affine maps preserve convex combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex outer function is evaluated after an affine transformation and may be added to another proper convex term; joint domain feasibility makes the resulting objective proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Composite Objectives

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Affine Sets and Convex Sets p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothness and Curvature Transfer Through an Affine Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative differential properties of one affine-composite component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) be linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^p\), and let \(h:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\) have an \(L_h\)-Lipschitz gradient. Then
\[
\nabla[h(Ax+b)]=A^{\mathsf T}\nabla h(Ax+b)
\]
and this gradient is \(L_h\|A\|_2^2\)-Lipschitz. If \(h\) is also \(\mu_h\)-strongly convex and \(A\) is injective, then \(h(Ax+b)\) is \(\mu_h\sigma_{\min}(A)^2\)-strongly convex. If \(A\) is not injective, the composite is constant along every direction in \(\ker A\), so strong convexity of \(h\) alone cannot yield strong convexity on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine precomposition scales smoothness by the squared operator norm and transfers strong convexity only when the linear map controls every direction.
assumptions_latex: The curvature conclusion additionally assumes \(h\) is \(\mu_h\)-strongly convex and \(A\) is injective.
knowledge_statements.title: Smoothness and Curvature Transfer Through an Affine Map

children.title: Multi-Operator Composite Objectives
children.top_down_role: Several transformed components coupled through distinct linear operators.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient and Lipschitz bound for smooth transformed components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If each \(h_i:Y_i\to\mathbb R\) has an \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient, then
\[
\Phi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m h_i(A_ix+b_i),\qquad
\nabla\Phi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^mA_i^*\nabla h_i(A_ix+b_i),
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla\Phi)\leq\sum_{i=1}^mL_i\|A_i\|^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transformed gradients add, and the sum of their operator-scaled smoothness constants is a valid global bound.
assumptions_latex: Every \(h_i\) is real-valued and has an \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient.
The spaces carry Euclidean inner products.

notation.meaning: Gradient-Lipschitz constant of the ith outer component.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Smoothness Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multi-Operator Composite Objective and Product-Space Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite sum of proper convex components acting through distinct affine operators and its stacked equivalent formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y_i\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(h_i:Y_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex, and let \(A_i:X\to Y_i\) be linear with \(b_i\in Y_i\). Define
\[
F(x)=g(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m h_i(A_ix+b_i).
\]
If some \(x\in\operatorname{dom}g\) satisfies \(A_ix+b_i\in\operatorname{dom}h_i\) for every \(i\), then \(F\) is proper convex. On \(Y=\prod_iY_i\), set \(\mathcal Ax=(A_1x,\ldots,A_mx)\), \(b=(b_1,\ldots,b_m)\), and \(H(y)=\sum_i h_i(y_i)\). Then
\[
F(x)=g(x)+H(\mathcal Ax+b),\qquad \mathcal A^*(y_1,\ldots,y_m)=\sum_iA_i^*y_i.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite multi-operator sum is proper convex under joint domain feasibility and is exactly one affine composite after product-space stacking.
assumptions_latex: The component domains are jointly feasible through the affine maps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is proper convex and }F=g+H\circ(\mathcal A\cdot+b).
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Operator Composite Objective and Product-Space Form
Multi-Operator Composite Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive convex components composed with distinct linear or affine operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), and for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(Y_i\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, \(A_i:X\to Y_i\) linear, \(b_i\in Y_i\), and \(h_i:Y_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) convex. A multi-operator composite objective has the representation \[F(x)=g(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{m}h_i(A_i x+b_i),\] with convex \(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). If some \(x\in\operatorname{dom}g\) satisfies \(A_i x+b_i\in\operatorname{dom}h_i\) for every \(i\), then \(F\) is proper and convex while retaining separate transformed-component structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct convex components act on separate affine images of one decision vector, and their sum is proper convex when all component domains are jointly feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(A_i:X\to Y_i\) is linear and \(b_i\in Y_i\) for every \(i\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite sums and affine precomposition preserve convexity under domain compatibility
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the terminal container, but no citation is supplied. Moreover, merely calling g and the h_i convex does not exclude improper extended-valued functions, so joint domain feasibility is insufficient for the stated properness conclusion; the components must be required to be proper convex functions.

children.title: Order-Preserving Convex Compositions
children.top_down_role: Nonlinear compositions governed by convexity-preserving monotonicity structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar failure of convexity under composition of two convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g(x)=x^2\) and \(h(t)=(t-1)^2\). Both functions are convex on \(\mathbb R\), but
\[
(h\circ g)(x)=(x^2-1)^2,
\qquad (h\circ g)''(0)=-4<0.
\]
Hence \(h\circ g\) is not convex; convexity of the inner and outer functions alone is insufficient when the outer function lacks compatible monotonicity on the inner range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two convex functions can have a nonconvex composition when the outer function lacks the required monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\circ g\text{ is not convex on }\mathbb R.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without Compatible Monotonicity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity-preserving nonlinear composition with coordinatewise matched monotonicity and inner curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex, let \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):C\to U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\), and let \(h:U\to\mathbb R\) be convex. Partition the coordinates into \(I_+\), \(I_-\), and \(I_0\). Suppose \(h\) is nondecreasing in each coordinate in \(I_+\), nonincreasing in each coordinate in \(I_-\), and unrestricted in coordinates in \(I_0\). If \(g_i\) is convex for \(i\in I_+\), concave for \(i\in I_-\), and affine for \(i\in I_0\), then \(h\circ g\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex outer function preserves convexity when each inner coordinate's curvature matches the outer function's monotonicity; affine coordinates need no monotonicity.
assumptions_latex: Outer monotonicity and inner curvature are paired coordinatewise as stated.
knowledge_statements.title: Signed Coordinatewise Convex Composition Rule
Order-Preserving Convex Compositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar convexity rule for a coordinatewise nondecreasing convex outer function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(g_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and write \(g(x)=(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\). Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be convex with \(g(C)\subseteq U\), and let \(h:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing: whenever \(u,v\in U\) and \(u_i\leq v_i\) for all \(i\), one has \(h(u)\leq h(v)\). Then the nonlinear composition \[F(x):=h(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\] is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex outer function that is nondecreasing in every coordinate preserves convexity when applied to a vector of convex inner functions.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing on \(U\)

notation.meaning: convex domain of the outer function

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard monotone convex composition rule
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

However, no source with a theorem or section locator is supplied, so the candidate requires an authoritative citation before review acceptance.

children.title: Finite-Sum Objectives
children.top_down_role: Component-indexed sums supporting full, incremental, or sampled access.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite component-average model with full, indexed, and sampled access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\ge1\) and let each \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, with \(\bigcap_{i=1}^N\operatorname{dom}f_i\ne\varnothing\). A convex finite-sum objective is \[F(x)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x).\] Then \(F\) is proper and convex. Full access evaluates all components, incremental access selects a specified index, and sampled access draws an index from a stated distribution. A positively weighted finite sum has the same architecture after absorbing its weights or normalization into the components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-sum objective averages proper convex components with a common effective-domain point and supports full, indexed, or sampled component access.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F=N^{-1}\sum_i f_i\text{ is proper and convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Proper Convex Finite-Sum Objective

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aggregation of Smoothness and Strong Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural constants inherited by a finite average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F=N^{-1}\sum_i f_i\), if each \(f_i\) is differentiable with an \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient, then \(\nabla F=N^{-1}\sum_i\nabla f_i\) is Lipschitz with valid constant \(\bar L=N^{-1}\sum_iL_i\). If each \(f_i\) is \(\mu_i\)-strongly convex, then \(F\) is \(\bar\mu\)-strongly convex for \(\bar\mu=N^{-1}\sum_i\mu_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite average inherits averaged valid smoothness and strong-convexity constants.
assumptions_latex: The smoothness conclusion assumes every \(f_i\) is differentiable with \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient
The strong-convexity conclusion assumes every \(f_i\) is \(\mu_i\)-strongly convex
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation of Smoothness and Strong Convexity

knowledge_statements.title: Unbiased Component and Mini-Batch Gradient Oracles
Finite-Sum Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite component-average model with explicit component-indexed oracle access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(N\in\mathbb{N}\). A finite-sum objective has the form \[F(x):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i(x),\qquad \min_{x\in X}F(x),\] where each \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex and the common domain \(\bigcap_{i=1}^{N}\operatorname{dom}f_i\) is nonempty. Full access evaluates all components, incremental access selects a specified index, and sampled access draws an index according to a stated distribution. Replacing the average by a positively weighted finite sum gives the same architecture after rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective averages finitely many convex components and supports full, indexed, or sampled component access.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}f_i\) is a proper convex finite-sum objective.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-sum convex objectives and component-indexed access are standard optimization models

children.title: Separability Structure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Decompositions aligned with variables, prescribed blocks, or scenario partitions.

children.title: Coordinatewise Separability
children.top_down_role: Objective decompositions aligned with individual variables or coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive separability with one univariate term per coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\prod_{j=1}^nX_j\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). A function \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is coordinatewise separable if \[F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=c+\sum_{j=1}^n\phi_j(x_j)\] for some \(c\in\mathbb R\) and univariate functions \(\phi_j:X_j\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). If every \(\phi_j\) is proper convex, then \(F\) is proper convex and minimization over \(X\) separates into scalar problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinatewise-separable function is a sum of univariate coordinate terms, so minimization on the matching Cartesian domain splits into scalar problems.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\phi_j\) is proper convex for the convexity and properness conclusion
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Separability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable diagnostic and convex counterexample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\in C^2\) is coordinatewise separable on an open rectangle, then \(\partial^2F/(\partial x_i\partial x_j)=0\) for all \(i\ne j\). Therefore \(F(x_1,x_2)=(x_1-x_2)^2\) is convex but not coordinatewise separable because its mixed derivative is \(-2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonzero mixed partials rule out coordinatewise additive separability; convexity alone does not imply separability.
assumptions_latex: \(F\in C^2\) on an open rectangle for the mixed-partial test
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Terms Obstruct Coordinatewise Separability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-coordinate geometry of a separable convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F(x)=c+\sum_{j=1}^n\phi_j(x_j)\) with proper convex \(\phi_j\), then \[\partial F(x)=\prod_{j=1}^n\partial\phi_j(x_j).\] Thus \(x^\star\) minimizes \(F\) on the Cartesian domain exactly when \(0\in\partial\phi_j(x_j^\star)\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global convex optimality reduces to one scalar subgradient condition per coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Subdifferential and Optimality

children.title: Blockwise Separability
children.top_down_role: Objective decompositions aligned with prescribed variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive separability over a prescribed product of variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\prod_{b=1}^B X_b\). A function \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is blockwise separable relative to this decomposition if \[F(x_1,\ldots,x_B)=c+\sum_{b=1}^B F_b(x_b)\] for some \(c\in\mathbb R\) and functions \(F_b:X_b\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). If every \(F_b\) is proper convex, then \(F\) is proper convex and \[\inf_{x\in X}F(x)=c+\sum_{b=1}^B\inf_{u\in X_b}F_b(u).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A blockwise-separable function is a sum of terms on disjoint variable blocks, and minimization over the matching product domain separates by block.
assumptions_latex: Each \(F_b\) is proper convex for the convexity and properness conclusion

notation.meaning: component depending only on block b

knowledge_statements.title: Blockwise Separability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between objective separability and optimization decomposability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An additively block-separable objective need not yield independent subproblems when the feasible set is not a Cartesian product. For example, \[\min_{x_1+x_2=1}x_1^2+x_2^2\] has solution \((1/2,1/2)\), whereas independent minimization of the two terms gives the infeasible point \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective separability alone does not overcome constraints that couple the variable blocks.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set may contain cross-block constraints
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Direct block decomposition requires compatible product feasibility, not merely an additive objective.}
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Block Constraints Destroy Direct Decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order geometry of a block-separable convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=c+\sum_{b=1}^B F_b(x_b)\) with proper convex components, \[\partial F(x)=\partial F_1(x_1)\times\cdots\times\partial F_B(x_B).\] Hence \(x^\star\) minimizes \(F\) over the product domain exactly when \(0\in\partial F_b(x_b^\star)\) for every block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The global subdifferential and optimality test split into independent block conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Product Subdifferential and Block Optimality

children.title: Scenario-Partitioned Separability
children.top_down_role: Objective decompositions organized by scenarios, samples, or partitioned data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive decomposition of an objective by scenarios, samples, or data partitions while retaining a shared decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite scenario set, let \(p_s\ge0\) with \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\), and let \(\ell_s:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). A scenario-partitioned objective has the form \[F(x)=\sum_{s\in S}p_s\ell_s(x).\] More generally, for a partition \(S=S_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}S_K\), define \(F_k(x)=\sum_{s\in S_k}p_s\ell_s(x)\); then \(F=\sum_{k=1}^KF_k\). If the positively weighted losses are proper convex and have a common domain point, then \(F\) is proper convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario-partitioned objective groups weighted scenario or sample losses while all groups may depend on the same decision.
assumptions_latex: The positively weighted proper convex losses have a common domain point for properness

notation.meaning: one block in a partition of the scenario or sample index set
aggregate loss contributed by scenario block k

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Partitioned Objective

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scenario Evaluation Separability Does Not Imply Decision Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes partitioned summand evaluation from independent scenario decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because all scenario losses may share \(x\), scenario-partitioned evaluation does not generally decompose minimization. For example, \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R}\tfrac12(x-1)^2+\tfrac12(x+1)^2\] has the shared-decision minimizer \(x=0\), whereas minimizing the two scenario losses independently gives the incompatible decisions \(1\) and \(-1\). Independent scenario subproblems arise only after introducing scenario-specific copies together with an explicit treatment of consensus or nonanticipativity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario losses can be evaluated separately even though their common decision prevents independent minimization.
assumptions_latex: Multiple scenario losses depend on a shared decision
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Summand separability does not imply independent scenario minimization when decisions are shared or nonanticipative.}
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Evaluation Separability Does Not Imply Decision Decomposition
Scenario-Partitioned Separability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted additive separability across scenario-specific variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite scenario set, let \(X=prod_{sin S}X_s\), and let weights \(p_s>0\) satisfy \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\). A function \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is scenario-partitioned separable if \[F((x_s)_{s\in S})=sum_{sin S}p_s F_s(x_s),\] where each \(F_s:X_s\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) depends only on its scenario block. If all \(F_s\) are proper and convex with nonempty domains, then \(F\) is proper and convex, and unconstrained minimization over the product set decomposes by scenario. Shared variables or cross-scenario constraints destroy this direct decomposition unless handled separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted scenario objective is separable when each term uses only its own scenario variables; coupling constraints or shared variables prevent direct decomposition.
assumptions_latex: Each \(F_s\) is proper and convex with nonempty domain

shared-variable convention may require taxonomy-level confirmation

children.title: Finite-Max Models
children.top_down_role: Pointwise maxima of finitely many convex components.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Max Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise maximum of finitely many proper convex component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f_i:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where \(m\in\mathbb{N}\). A finite-max objective has the representation \[F(x):=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x).\] The function \(F\) is convex on \(C\). It is proper whenever there exists \(x\in C\) at which every \(f_i(x)\) is finite and no component takes the value \(-\infty\). Equivalently, its epigraph satisfies \[\operatorname{epi}F=\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{epi}f_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise maximum of finitely many convex functions is convex, and its epigraph is the intersection of their epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i\) is proper and convex, with \(\operatorname{epi}F=\bigcap_i\operatorname{epi}f_i\).

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

review_flags: finite-max and epigraph details require locator confirmation

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz and strong-convexity properties inherited by a finite maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If each \(f_i\) is \(L_i\)-Lipschitz on \(C\), then \(F=\max_i f_i\) is \(\max_i L_i\)-Lipschitz on \(C\). If each \(f_i\) is \(\mu_i\)-strongly convex on the convex set \(C\), then \(F\) is \(\min_i\mu_i\)-strongly convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximum inherits the largest component Lipschitz bound and the smallest component strong-convexity modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex for the strong-convexity assertion
The stated component moduli hold uniformly on \(C\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is }(\max_iL_i)\text{-Lipschitz and, when applicable, }(\min_i\mu_i)\text{-strongly convex}.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz and strong-convexity moduli of component i

knowledge_statements.title: Inheritance of Uniform Regularity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact auxiliary-variable formulation of finite-max minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\), \[\inf_{x\in C}F(x)=\inf\{t:x\in C,\ t\in\mathbb R,\ f_i(x)\le t\ \text{for all }i\}.\] If the finite optimum is attained, \((x^\star,t^\star)\) is optimal exactly when \(x^\star\) minimizes \(F\) and \(t^\star=F(x^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One epigraph variable converts finite-max minimization into simultaneous component inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in C}\max_i f_i(x)=\inf\{t:x\in C,\ f_i(x)\le t\ \forall i\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Reformulation of Finite-Max Minimization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex Representation of a Finite Maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent finite-dimensional supremum representation when all component values are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a\in\mathbb R^m\), \[\max_i a_i=\max_{p\in\Delta_m}\sum_{i=1}^m p_i a_i,\qquad \Delta_m=\{p\in\mathbb R_+^m:\mathbf1^Tp=1\}.\] Thus, wherever every \(f_i(x)\) is finite, \(F(x)=\max_{p\in\Delta_m}\sum_i p_i f_i(x)\), and an active index supplies an optimal simplex vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximum of finite values equals maximization of their convex combinations over the probability simplex.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i\in\mathbb R\), or equivalently every \(f_i(x)\) is finite at the point considered
knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Representation of a Finite Maximum

children.top_down_role: Supremum representations generated by convex sets.

\(A:X\to Y\) is linear and \(b\in Y\) for the affine-composite model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supremal convex representation induced by a nonempty set of linear coefficients.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(Y=\mathbb{R}^p\) with its Euclidean inner product, and let \(C\subseteq Y\) be nonempty. The support function generated by \(C\) is \[\sigma_C(y):=\sup_{u\in C}\langle u,y\rangle,\qquad y\in Y.\] It is a proper, lower-semicontinuous, positively homogeneous convex function, possibly taking the value \(+\infty\), and satisfies \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C}\). Consequently, for any linear map \(A:X\to Y\) and any \(b\in Y\), the extended-real-valued function \(x\mapsto\sigma_C(Ax+b)\) is convex on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support function is the supremum of linear forms indexed by a nonempty set; it is a proper closed convex function, depends only on the set's closed convex hull, and remains convex after affine precomposition.
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Models

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed-face certificate for a closed convex generating set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) is nonempty, closed, and convex and \(\sigma_C(y)<+\infty\), then \[\partial\sigma_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in C}\langle u,y\rangle.\] Thus a maximizing \(u\) certifies the support value and is a subgradient; both sets can be empty when the finite supremum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support-function subgradients are exactly the maximizing points of the closed convex generating set.
knowledge_statements.title: Attained Support and Subgradients

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global and directional finiteness boundaries for support functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^p\), \(\sigma_C\) is finite everywhere if and only if \(C\) is bounded. If \(C\) is also closed, this is equivalent to compactness. For a fixed \(y\), \(\sigma_C(y)<+\infty\) exactly when \(u\mapsto\langle u,y\rangle\) is bounded above on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support function is finite in every direction exactly when its generating set is bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Finiteness and Boundedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling, Minkowski sums, and linear images translated into support-function operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^p\), \(\alpha>0\), and a linear map \(A\), \[\sigma_{\alpha C}=\alpha\sigma_C,\qquad \sigma_{C+D}=\sigma_C+\sigma_D,\qquad \sigma_{AC}(y)=\sigma_C(A^Ty).\] For \(\alpha=0\), \(0C=\{0\}\) and \(\sigma_{0C}\equiv0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling, Minkowski addition, and linear imaging become scaling, addition, and adjoint precomposition of support functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Set Calculus

children.title: Saddle-Representable Objectives
children.top_down_role: Supremum representations exposing explicit dual variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Saddle-Representable Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex supremum representation with an explicit dual variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(Y_0\subseteq Y\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(\Phi:X\times Y_0\to\mathbb{R}\). The objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is saddle-representable when
\[
f(x)=\sup_{y\in Y_0}\Phi(x,y),
\]
where \(x\mapsto\Phi(x,y)\) is closed and convex for every \(y\in Y_0\), while \(y\mapsto\Phi(x,y)\) is concave for every \(x\in X\). Then \(f\) is convex, and \(y\) is the explicit dual variable in the representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle-representable objective is the supremum, over an explicit convex dual domain, of functions that are convex in the primal variable and concave in the dual variable; the resulting objective is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
For each \(y\in Y_0\), \(\Phi(\cdot,y)\) is closed and convex; for each \(x\in X\), \(\Phi(x,\cdot)\) is concave.

notation.meaning: Feasible domain of the explicit dual variable.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes closed convex representability from properness and dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the seed assumptions, \(f=\sup_{y\in Y_0}\Phi(\cdot,y)\) is closed and convex, but it is proper only if it is finite at some primal point. Supremum attainment requires additional assumptions: for \(Y_0=(0,1)\) and \(\Phi(x,y)=y\), one has \(f(x)=1\) for every \(x\), but no maximizing \(y\in Y_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convexity does not guarantee properness or existence of a maximizing dual variable.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\Phi(\cdot,y)\) is real-valued, closed, and convex
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is proper iff it is finite somewhere; dual attainment needs additional compactness or coercivity-type assumptions}.
knowledge_statements.title: Properness and Supremum-Attainment Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact epigraph description of a supremal saddle representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f(x)=\sup_{y\in Y_0}\Phi(x,y)\), then \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):\Phi(x,y)\le t\text{ for every }y\in Y_0\}=\bigcap_{y\in Y_0}\operatorname{epi}\Phi(\cdot,y).\] Hence minimizing \(f\) is equivalent to minimizing \(t\) subject to these indexed inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph is the intersection of all inequalities indexed by the explicit dual variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Indexed Epigraph Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence under scalar transformations of objective and constraint functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to standard-form optimization without requiring convexity. Equality of optimal-point sets requires the objective transformation to be strictly increasing; a merely nondecreasing transformation can introduce additional minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\psi_0:\mathbf R\to\mathbf R\) be strictly increasing. For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), suppose \(\psi_i(u)\leq0\iff u\leq0\), and for \(i=m+1,\ldots,m+p\), suppose \(\psi_i(u)=0\iff u=0\). Define \(\widetilde f_i=\psi_i\circ f_i\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\) and \(\widetilde h_i=\psi_{m+i}\circ h_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,p\). Then the transformed and original problems have identical feasible sets and identical optimal-point sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictly increasing transformation of the objective, together with transformations preserving the nonpositive sets of inequalities and the zero sets of equalities, leaves the feasible set and the set of minimizers unchanged. Mere nondecreasing monotonicity is insufficient for equality of minimizer sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence of explicit constraints and extended-valued objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encodes a feasible set in an extended-valued objective and conversely exposes effective-domain restrictions as explicit constraints, while preserving the source's smoothness failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f_0:f_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ h_j(x)=0,\ j=1,\ldots,p\}\), and define \(F(x)=f_0(x)\) for \(x\in C\) and \(F(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Then unconstrained minimization of \(F\) is equivalent to minimizing \(f_0\) over \(C\): the formulations have the same finite admissible points, optimal points, and optimal value. Conversely, an effective-domain restriction of an extended-valued objective can be exposed as an explicit constraint. This optimization equivalence need not preserve ordinary smoothness of the objective representation; restricting a differentiable objective to a set that is not open can yield an extended-valued objective that is not differentiable in the ordinary real-valued sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit constraints can be absorbed into the objective by assigning infinity outside the feasible set, without changing the finite admissible points, optimizers, or optimal value. A restriction hidden in an extended-valued objective can conversely be written as an explicit constraint. The optimization problems are equivalent, but ordinary differentiability need not be preserved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x}F(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f_0(x),\qquad \inf_xF(x)=\inf_{x\in C}f_0(x),\quad\text{while ordinary objective smoothness need not be preserved by the encoding.}

children.title: Indicator-Function Models
children.top_down_role: Hard constraints represented by set-generated objective components.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator-Function Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real encoding of a hard convex constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real vector space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty. The indicator function of \(C\) is
\[
\delta_C(x)=
\begin{cases}
0,&x\in C,\\
+\infty,&x\notin C.
\end{cases}
\]
For every \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\),
\[
\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+\delta_C(x)\bigr)=\inf_{x\in C}f(x).
\]
If \(f(x_0)<+\infty\) for some \(x_0\in C\), the two formulations also have exactly the same global minimizers. If \(C\) is convex, then \(\delta_C\) is convex; if \(C\) is also closed, then \(\delta_C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator is zero on the constraint set and infinite outside it, so adding it exactly encodes the hard constraint in the objective; minimizers also coincide when the objective is finite at some feasible point.
assumptions_latex: For minimizer equivalence, there exists \(x_0\in C\) with \(f(x_0)<+\infty\).
For convexity, \(C\) is convex; for closedness, \(C\) is additionally closed.

notation.meaning: Extended-real indicator function of the set.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Minimization with Functional Constraints p. 204

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.4 Minimization with Functional Constraints p. 204

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real algebra for combining finitely many hard membership constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq X\), \[\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_{C_i}(x)=\delta_{\cap_{i=1}^m C_i}(x)\qquad(x\in X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding finitely many indicator functions combines hard constraints by intersecting their sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Algebra for Intersections

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indicator Subdifferential as a Normal Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order geometry intrinsic to a convex indicator model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional inner-product space. For \(x\in C\), \[\partial\delta_C(x)=N_C(x):=\{u:\langle u,z-x\rangle\le0\ \text{for all }z\in C\},\] while \(\partial\delta_C(x)=\varnothing\) for \(x\notin C\). Whenever the convex subdifferential sum rule applies, minimizing a proper convex \(f\) over \(C\) is characterized by \(0\in\partial f(x)+N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a convex-set indicator is its normal cone, converting constrained optimality into a normal-cone inclusion.
assumptions_latex: For the summed optimality formula, the convex subdifferential sum rule applies.

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic normal cone to the set.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Subdifferential as a Normal Cone

children.title: Set-Distance Penalties
children.top_down_role: Soft constraint encodings based on displacement from a convex feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Distance Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soft constraint penalty generated by distance to a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,\|\cdot\|)\) be a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty and closed. Define
\[
d_C(x)=\inf_{z\in C}\|x-z\|,
\qquad P_\rho(x)=\rho d_C(x),
\]
for \(\rho>0\). Then \(P_\rho(x)\geq0\), and \(P_\rho(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\in C\). If \(C\) is convex, \(d_C\), and hence \(P_\rho\), is convex. Moreover, \(d_C\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz with respect to \(\|\cdot\|\), so \(P_\rho\) is \(\rho\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-distance penalty charges a positive multiple of distance from the constraint set; it vanishes exactly on the set and is convex for convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_\rho=\rho d_C\) vanishes exactly on \(C\), and is convex when \(C\) is convex.

notation.meaning: Distance to the set under the given norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-Norm Representation of Distance to a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-function representation of norm distance in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space, with dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\). Then \[d_C(x)=\sup_{\|u\|_*\le1}\bigl(\langle u,x\rangle-\sigma_C(u)\bigr),\qquad \sigma_C(u)=\sup_{z\in C}\langle u,z\rangle.\] Consequently, \(\rho d_C\) is the supremum of these affine functions over \(\|u\|_*\le\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a closed convex set is the supremum of support-function deficits over the dual unit ball.
assumptions_latex: The space is finite-dimensional and normed.

notation.meaning: Support function of the constraint set.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Norm Representation of Distance to a Convex Set

children.title: Residual Violation Penalties
children.top_down_role: Soft encodings built from scalar or vector measures of constraint violation.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Violation Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-part penalties for scalar convex inequality residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real vector space and let \(g_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). For weights \(\rho_i>0\), define the residual violation penalty
\[
P(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\rho_i[g_i(x)]_+,
\qquad [t]_+=\max\{t,0\}.
\]
Then \(P:X\to\mathbb{R}_+\) is convex, and \(P(x)=0\) if and only if every inequality \(g_i(x)\leq0\) holds. Thus adding \(P\) to an objective softly penalizes the magnitude of violated inequality residuals while assigning no charge to satisfied inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted sum of positive constraint residuals is convex, vanishes precisely at points satisfying all inequalities, and penalizes only violations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is convex and \(P(x)=0\iff g_i(x)\leq0\) for every \(i\).

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Minimization with Functional Constraints p. 204

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.4 Minimization with Functional Constraints p. 204

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm penalties for affine equality violations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an affine equality system \(Ax=b\), a norm \(\|\cdot\|\), and \(\rho>0\), \[P_\rho(x)=\rho\|Ax-b\|\] is convex and satisfies \(P_\rho(x)=0\iff Ax=b\). For a scalar affine equality this becomes \(\rho|a^Tx-\beta|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm of an affine equality residual is convex and vanishes exactly on the equality-feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality Residual Penalties

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued aggregation of positive inequality residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:X\to\mathbb R^m\) have convex components and set \(G_+(x)=([G_1(x)]_+,\ldots,[G_m(x)]_+)\). If \(\|\cdot\|_a\) is a norm monotone on the nonnegative orthant, then for \(\rho>0\), \[P_\rho(x)=\rho\|G_+(x)\|_a\] is convex and vanishes exactly when \(G(x)\le0\). Weighted sums and maximum violations arise from weighted \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_\infty\) norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone norm of the positive residual vector gives a convex violation penalty; sums and worst-constraint penalties are special cases.
assumptions_latex: \(\|\cdot\|_a\) is a norm monotone on \(\mathbb R_+^m\).

notation.meaning: Componentwise positive part of the residual vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Vector Residual Norm Penalties

children.title: Penalty Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where distance penalties and violation penalties do or do not represent comparable constraint geometry.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing Residuals Need Not Control Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of residual-distance comparability without an error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{0\}\subset\mathbb R\) and \(v(x)=x^2\). Although \(v^{-1}(0)=C\), no finite \(\kappa\) and no neighborhood of zero satisfy \[d_C(x)=|x|\le\kappa v(x)=\kappa x^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A violation function may have exactly the feasible zero set yet be too flat to dominate distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing Residuals Need Not Control Distance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Error Bounds Transfer Residual Penalties to Distance Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regional quantitative condition under which a residual violation dominates distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\ne\varnothing\), let \(v:X\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfy \(v^{-1}(0)=C\), and suppose \[d_C(x)\le\kappa v(x)\qquad(x\in S).\] If \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(S\cup C\), every \(x\in S\) has a nearest point in \(C\), and a constrained minimizer exists, then for \(\rho>L\kappa\), \[x\in S\setminus C\Longrightarrow f(x)+\rho v(x)>\min_{z\in C}f(z).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual-to-distance error bound and Lipschitz objective make a sufficiently large residual penalty exclude infeasible minimizers on the region where the bound holds.
assumptions_latex: Nearest points in \(C\) exist for points of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in S\setminus C\Longrightarrow f(x)+\rho v(x)>\min_{z\in C}f(z).
knowledge_statements.title: Error Bounds Transfer Residual Penalties to Distance Penalties

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictness of the Lipschitz Exact-Penalty Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for a linear distance penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{0\}\subset\mathbb R\), \(f(x)=-Lx\) with \(L>0\), and \(P_\rho(x)=-Lx+\rho|x|\). The constrained minimizer is \(0\). If \(\rho=L\), every \(x\ge0\) minimizes \(P_\rho\), including infeasible points; if \(0\le\rho<L\), then \(\inf_xP_\rho(x)=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strict penalty-weight threshold cannot generally be weakened to equality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho=L\text{ permits infeasible minimizers, while }0\le\rho<L\text{ gives unboundedness below}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness of the Lipschitz Exact-Penalty Threshold

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal-Multiplier Threshold for an Exact Residual Penalty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite exactness threshold supplied by an attained nonnegative optimal multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(p^*=\min\{f(x):g_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), where \(f,g_i\) are convex. Suppose \(x^*\) is primal optimal and \(\lambda^*\ge0\) is dual optimal with \(p^*=\inf_x\{f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i^*g_i(x)\}\). Define \(P_\rho(x)=f(x)+\rho\sum_i[g_i(x)]_+\). If \(\rho\ge\|\lambda^*\|_\infty\), then \(\inf_xP_\rho(x)=p^*\) and every constrained minimizer minimizes \(P_\rho\). If \(\rho>\|\lambda^*\|_\infty\), every minimizer of \(P_\rho\), when one exists, is feasible and hence constrained-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attained optimal multiplier gives a finite exact-penalty threshold; strict domination of its components excludes infeasible penalized minimizers.
assumptions_latex: A primal optimizer \(x^*\) and nonnegative dual optimizer \(\lambda^*\) exist with zero duality gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Multiplier Threshold for an Exact Residual Penalty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Recovery by Diverging Penalty Weights
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cluster-point recovery for a nonnegative violation penalty as its weight diverges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v:X\to[0,+\infty]\) satisfy \(C=\{x:v(x)=0\}\ne\varnothing\), and let \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) with \(f(x^*)<+\infty\). For \(\rho_k\to+\infty\), let \(x_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{f(x)+\rho_kv(x)\}\). If \(\{x_k\}\) lies in a compact set \(K\), \(f\) and \(v\) are lower semicontinuous, and \(f\) is finite and bounded below on \(K\), then \(v(x_k)\to0\), and every cluster point of \(\{x_k\}\) minimizes \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under compactness and lower-semicontinuity assumptions, minimizers for diverging penalty weights have only constrained-optimal cluster points, even when no finite weight is exact.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho_k\to+\infty\), and each penalized problem has a minimizer \(x_k\).
\(f\) and \(v\) are lower semicontinuous, and \(f\) is finite and bounded below on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Recovery by Diverging Penalty Weights
Penalty Equivalence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between asymptotic soft penalties and finite exact penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider minimizing \(f(x)\) over a nonempty closed set \(C\) and the penalized objectives \(f(x)+\rho d_C(x)^p\), where \(p>1\). Even for convex data, no finite \(\rho\) need reproduce the constrained minimizer. Specifically, on \(X=\mathbb{R}\), take \(C=\{0\}\), \(f(x)=-x\), and \(p>1\). The constrained minimizer is \(0\), whereas
\[
\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\{-x+\rho|x|^p\}
\]
is attained at \(x=(\rho p)^{-1/(p-1)}>0\) for every finite \(\rho>0\). Thus superlinear distance penalties generally enforce feasibility only asymptotically, unlike linear exact penalties under suitable regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A superlinear distance penalty need not be exact at any finite weight: a linear objective over a singleton constraint supplies a concrete convex counterexample.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every finite \(\rho>0\), the penalized minimizer is positive and therefore infeasible.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample and stated minimizer are mathematically correct and fit a failure-boundary container, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the asserted general boundary between superlinear and exact linear penalties.

children.title: Exact-Penalty Families
children.top_down_role: Convex penalty families organized by equivalence and threshold regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Penalty Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-threshold equivalence between constrained and penalized minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty, and let \(v:X\to\mathbb{R}_+\) satisfy \(v(x)=0\) exactly for \(x\in C\). The family
\[
F_\rho(x)=f(x)+\rho v(x),\qquad \rho>0,
\]
is an exact-penalty family for the constrained problem \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\) if there exists a finite threshold \(\bar\rho\geq0\) such that, for every \(\rho>\bar\rho\), the global minimizers of \(F_\rho\) coincide with the global constrained minimizers. Equality of optimal values then follows automatically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A penalty family is exact when every weight above one finite threshold yields exactly the constrained problem's global minimizers.
assumptions_latex: The constrained problem has at least one global minimizer.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Minimization with Functional Constraints p. 204

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.4 Minimization with Functional Constraints p. 204

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Threshold Equality Need Not Give Coincident Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary between primal optimality at the multiplier bound and coincidence of minimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{-x:x\le0\}\), the unique constrained minimizer is \(0\) and an optimal multiplier is \(1\). At \(\rho=1\), \[F_1(x)=-x+[x]_+=\begin{cases}-x,&x<0,\\0,&x\ge0,\end{cases}\] so \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_1=[0,+\infty)\), which contains infeasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the multiplier threshold, extra infeasible minimizers may remain even though every constrained solution minimizes the penalty objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Equality Need Not Give Coincident Minimizers

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplier Threshold for Convex Exact Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite exactness threshold certified by an optimal Lagrange multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min_x f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m.\] Suppose a primal optimum is attained and strong duality holds with an optimal multiplier \(\lambda^\star\ge0\). For \[F_\rho(x)=f(x)+\rho\sum_{i=1}^m[g_i(x)]_+,\] every primal solution minimizes \(F_\rho\) when \(\rho\ge\|\lambda^\star\|_\infty\). If \(\rho>\|\lambda^\star\|_\infty\), every global minimizer of \(F_\rho\) is feasible and therefore primal-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal multiplier supplies a sufficient finite threshold for the l1 violation penalty; strict inequality excludes infeasible penalized minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and the \(g_i\) are proper convex functions.
Strong duality holds with an optimal multiplier \(\lambda^\star\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Threshold for Convex Exact Penalties

children.title: Partial-Minimization Models
children.top_down_role: Marginal objectives obtained by eliminating auxiliary variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Minimization Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex marginal objective obtained by eliminating an auxiliary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, and let \(F:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and jointly convex. Define the marginal function
\[
g(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y).
\]
If \(g(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in X\), then \(g:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and convex. Even when \(F\) is closed, the marginal \(g\) need not be closed and the defining infimum need not be attained without additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization eliminates an auxiliary variable by taking an infimum. The resulting marginal is a proper convex objective when it never takes negative infinity, while closedness and attainment require additional conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(F:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\) is a proper convex function.

notation.meaning: Marginal objective after eliminating the auxiliary variable.

source_refs.locator: 3.3. Partial Minimization of Convex Functions p. 122

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3. Partial Minimization of Convex Functions p. 122

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inf-Compact Fibers Ensure Attainment and Closed Marginals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition preventing escape of eliminated variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and jointly convex on finite-dimensional spaces. Suppose that for every compact \(K\subset X\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), \[\{(x,y):x\in K,\ F(x,y)\le\alpha\}\] is compact. Then \(g(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\) is closed and convex, and its infimum is attained for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform inf-compactness in the eliminated variable yields a closed convex marginal with attained fiber minima.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and jointly convex.
The displayed sublevel sets over compact retained-variable sets are compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is closed and convex, and }\arg\min_yF(x,y)\ne\varnothing\text{ for }x\in\operatorname{dom}g.
knowledge_statements.title: Inf-Compact Fibers Ensure Attainment and Closed Marginals

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Joint Objective Can Have a Nonclosed Marginal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete closedness failure under projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\ge1/x\}.\] This set is closed and convex. For \(F=\delta_C\), \[g(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)=\begin{cases}0,&x>0,\\+\infty,&x\le0,\end{cases}\] so \(g=\delta_{(0,\infty)}\) is convex but not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex joint objective can project to an open effective domain, so partial minimization need not preserve closedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is closed convex but }g=\delta_{(0,\infty)}\text{ is not closed}.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Joint Objective Can Have a Nonclosed Marginal

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation obtained by setting the eliminated variable's dual coordinate to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\), with conjugates under the product pairing, \[g^*(x^*)=F^*(x^*,0).\] No attainment of the fiber infimum is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a marginal is the joint conjugate evaluated at zero in the eliminated variable's dual coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an extended-real function on \(X\times Y\).
Conjugates use the same product dual pairing.

notation.meaning: Zero dual coordinate for the eliminated variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate of a Marginal Function

children.title: Infimal-Convolution Models
children.top_down_role: Reduced objectives distributing structure across additive decompositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Infimal-Convolution Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive decomposition model for combining two extended-real objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, and let \(f,g:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper functions. Their infimal convolution is
\[
(f\mathbin{\square}g)(x)=\inf_{u+v=x}\{f(u)+g(v)\}=\inf_{u\in X}\{f(u)+g(x-u)\}.
\]
If \(f\) and \(g\) are convex and the displayed infimum never equals \(-\infty\), then \(f\mathbin{\square}g\) is convex. Moreover,
\[
(f\mathbin{\square}g)^*=f^*+g^*,
\]
where conjugates are taken with respect to the same dual pairing; no attainment assumption is needed for this conjugacy identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution splits a point into two additive components and minimizes the sum of their costs; for convex inputs it is convex and conjugates to a sum.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper convex functions on a finite-dimensional space.

notation.meaning: Infimal convolution of the two functions.

source_refs.locator: 4.5 Infimal Convolution and Conjugacy p. 102

source_witnesses.locator: 4.5 Infimal Convolution and Conjugacy p. 102

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient certificate for an attained additive decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g\) be proper closed convex functions and suppose \(x=u+v\) attains \((f\square g)(x)=f(u)+g(v)\). Then \[\partial(f\square g)(x)=\partial f(u)\cap\partial g(v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an attained optimal split, the subgradients of the infimal convolution are exactly the common subgradients of the component costs.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Decomposition Subgradient Condition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebra and Epigraph Geometry of Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic laws and the attainment-sensitive epigraph-sum formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Infimal convolution is commutative and associative whenever the extended-real expressions are defined: \[f\square g=g\square f,\qquad (f\square g)\square h=f\square(g\square h).\] Moreover, \[\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\subseteq\operatorname{epi}(f\square g).\] Equality holds when every finite decomposition infimum is attained. Without attainment, the inclusion can be strict and closure may be required to recover boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution is commutative and associative; the Minkowski sum of component epigraphs equals its epigraph under decomposition attainment and may omit boundary points otherwise.
assumptions_latex: The extended-real expressions involved are defined.
For epigraph equality, every finite decomposition infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Algebra and Epigraph Geometry of Infimal Convolution

children.title: Auxiliary-Variable Lifts
children.top_down_role: Lifted formulations that introduce variables to expose hidden component structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent lifted formulation whose auxiliary variables recover the original objective by elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(C\subseteq X\), and suppose an objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) admits
\[
f(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}\{F(x,y):G(x,y)\in K\},
\]
where \(K\) is a prescribed constraint set. Then
\[
\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf\{F(x,y):x\in C,\ y\in Y,\ G(x,y)\in K\}.
\]
If the inner infimum is attained for every feasible \(x\), projecting the lifted minimizers onto their \(x\)-coordinates yields exactly the minimizers of the original problem; conversely, every original minimizer has a minimizing auxiliary completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An auxiliary-variable lift replaces an objective by an equivalent higher-dimensional constrained model; eliminating auxiliaries recovers the original values and, under attainment, its minimizers.
assumptions_latex: The displayed marginal representation of \(f\) holds for every \(x\in C\).
The lifted feasible set is nonempty.
For minimizer equivalence, each relevant inner infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original and lifted problems have equal optimal values, and their minimizers correspond by projection under attainment.

notation.meaning: Constraint set used in the lift.
