knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex singular-value penalties designed to shrink the effective rank of a matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q=\min\{m,n\}\), and let \(\phi:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, absolutely symmetric, and coordinatewise nondecreasing on \(\mathbb R_+^q\). For \(\lambda>0\), a convex low-rank spectral penalty has the form
\[
R_\lambda(X)=\lambda\phi(\sigma(X)),\qquad X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}.
\]
It is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and unitarily invariant. The canonical choice \(\phi(s)=\lVert s\rVert_1\) yields \(R_\lambda(X)=\lambda\lVert X\rVert_*\); its nonsmoothness at zero singular values supports singular-value sparsity under suitable optimization models. The unregularized case may be defined separately by \(R_0(X)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex low-rank spectral penalties apply suitable symmetric convex functions to singular values; the nuclear norm is the canonical singular-value-sparsity penalty.
knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Spectral Penalties

children.title: Joint-Structure Tradeoffs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex additive regularization combining entrywise sparsity and low-rank penalties.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a proper convex loss \(L:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), an additive sparse-low-rank estimator may be represented by
\[
\min_{X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}}L(X)+\lambda_S\lVert X\rVert_{1,\mathrm{ent}}+\lambda_L\lVert X\rVert_*,
\qquad \lambda_S,\lambda_L\ge0.
\]
The objective is proper and convex. When both weights are positive, \(\lambda_S/\lambda_L\) specifies the relative coefficients of the entrywise and spectral penalties, while multiplying both weights by a common positive factor changes their common scale relative to the loss. The resulting optimizer's sparsity and rank can also depend on \(L\) and the data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding entrywise l1 and nuclear norms gives a proper convex objective. Their ratio specifies relative penalty coefficients, but the optimizer's actual sparsity and rank also depend on the loss and data.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint-Structure Tradeoffs

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability boundary for additive sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a coordinate matrix \(E_{ij}=e_ie_j^\top\), \[\|E_{ij}\|_{1,\mathrm{ent}}=\|E_{ij}\|_*=1.\] In the decomposition \(X=S+M\) with \(X=E_{ij}\) and \(\lambda_S=\lambda_L>0\), every split \[(S,M)=(tE_{ij},(1-t)E_{ij}),\qquad0\le t\le1,\] has the same regularization cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate rank-one matrix is simultaneously sparse and low rank, so additive penalties alone need not identify its decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The sparse-plus-low-rank decomposition is nonunique without additional information}.

notation.meaning: Matrix with one unit entry at \((i,j)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse and Low-Rank Atoms Overlap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Latent decomposition alternative to imposing both penalties on one matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex. The model \[\min_{S,M}\ L(S+M)+\lambda_S\|S\|_{1,\mathrm{ent}}+\lambda_L\|M\|_*\qquad(\lambda_S,\lambda_L\ge0)\] is convex. Eliminating \(S,M\) induces the infimal-convolution regularizer \[R(X)=\inf_{S+M=X}\{\lambda_S\|S\|_{1,\mathrm{ent}}+\lambda_L\|M\|_*\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate sparse and low-rank latent matrices produce a convex decomposition model and an infimal-convolution penalty on their sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Plus-Low-Rank Decomposition Model

children.title: Indicator Regularizers
children.top_down_role: Set membership represented as an extended-valued regularizer.

assumptions_latex: For lower-semicontinuity and convexity of \(\delta_C\), the set \(C\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}(f(x)+\delta_C(x))\), and \(\delta_C\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex exactly when \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
review_flags: All TeX commands in statement_latex were placed inside explicit math delimiters.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a hard convex constraint as an extended-valued objective term.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), its extended-valued indicator is
\[
\delta_C(x)=
\begin{cases}
0,&x\in C,\\
+\infty,&x\notin C.
\end{cases}
\]
Consequently, for any extended-real-valued objective \(f\), minimizing \(f(x)+\delta_C(x)\) over \(\mathbb R^n\) is equivalent, in feasible points and objective values, to minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(x\in C\). The indicator \(\delta_C\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex exactly when \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indicator regularizer equals zero on a constraint set and infinity outside, converting constrained minimization into unconstrained extended-valued minimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Regularizers

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic first-order certificate for a closed convex indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), \[\partial\delta_C(x)=N_C(x):=\{v:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\ \forall y\in C\}\quad(x\in C),\] while \(\partial\delta_C(x)=\varnothing\) for \(x\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a convex-set indicator is its normal cone.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Subdifferential of an Indicator

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indicator Algebra for Intersections and Positive Scaling

\delta_C\) for every \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding indicators combines hard constraints by intersection, and positive rescaling does not change an indicator.
knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Algebra for Intersections and Positive Scaling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-generated convex regularizers and their indicator-function conjugacy.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), its support function is
\[
\sigma_C(x):=\sup_{y\in C}\langle x,y\rangle,
\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n.
\]
The function \(\sigma_C\) is lower-semicontinuous, convex, and positively homogeneous, and it depends only on the closed convex hull of \(C\). For nonempty closed convex \(C\), Fenchel conjugacy gives
\[
\sigma_C=\delta_C^*.
\]
Consequently, \(\lambda\sigma_C\) is an extended-valued convex regularizer for every \(\lambda>0\). The unregularized case may be defined separately as the zero function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support-function regularizer maximizes a linear pairing over a set. For a nonempty closed convex set, the support function is the Fenchel conjugate of the set's indicator.
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Regularizers

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection Formula for the Proximal Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact proximal evaluation of a support-function penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, then for every \(\lambda>0\), \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\sigma_C}(x)=x-\lambda P_C(x/\lambda).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal map of a scaled support function is obtained using one projection onto its generating set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Formula for the Proximal Map

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order geometry of a support-function regularizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support-function subgradients are exactly the generating-set points attaining the defining linear maximum.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugating the support function recovers the closed convex generating set's indicator.

children.title: Distance-to-Set Regularizers
children.top_down_role: Regularizers based on displacement from a prescribed convex set.

assumptions_latex: For convexity and uniqueness of projection, \(C\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For nonempty closed convex \(C\), \(R_\lambda(x)=\lambda\lVert x-P_Cx\rVert_2\) is convex and \(\lambda\)-Lipschitz.

notation.meaning: Unique Euclidean projection of x onto C.

review_flags: Projection, convexity, and Lipschitz properties require confirmation against a more specific source locator.
All TeX commands in statement_latex were placed inside explicit math delimiters.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean distance penalty generated by a nonempty closed convex set.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
d_C(x):=\inf_{y\in C}\lVert x-y\rVert_2,
\qquad
R_\lambda(x):=\lambda d_C(x),\quad \lambda\ge0.
\]
Then \(d_C(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\in C\), and \(d_C\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz. If \(C\) is also convex, then \(d_C\) is convex and the infimum is attained at the unique Euclidean projection \(P_Cx\), so \(d_C(x)=\lVert x-P_Cx\rVert_2\). Thus the finite penalty measures constraint violation without imposing hard feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance-to-set regularization penalizes Euclidean constraint violation; for nonempty closed convex sets it is convex, Lipschitz, and computed by the unique Euclidean projection.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance-to-Set Regularizers

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order characterization of a convex distance penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. If \(x\notin C\), then \(d_C\) is differentiable at \(x\) and \[\nabla d_C(x)=\frac{x-P_Cx}{\|x-P_Cx\|_2}.\] If \(x\in C\), then \(\partial d_C(x)=N_C(x)\cap B_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside a closed convex set, the distance gradient is the unit projection residual; on the set, its subgradients are unit-bounded normals.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential of Convex Distance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate of Distance to a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel dual representation of Euclidean distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, then \[d_C^*(z)=\sigma_C(z)+\delta_{\{z:\|z\|_2\le1\}}(z).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of distance is the support function of the set restricted to the Euclidean unit ball.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate of Distance to a Convex Set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent convex representation of distance to a set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\), \[d_C(x)=\inf_y\{\|x-y\|_2+\delta_C(y)\}=(\|\cdot\|_2\square\delta_C)(x).\] For closed convex \(C\), this is a finite closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a set is the infimal convolution of the Euclidean norm and the set indicator.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance as Infimal Convolution

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient and sharp Lipschitz threshold for recovery of a hard constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be globally \(L\)-Lipschitz. If \(\lambda>L\), then \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\bigl(f(x)+\lambda d_C(x)\bigr)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x).\] The strict inequality is sharp: if \(C=\{0\}\), \(f(x)=-L|x|\), and \(\lambda=L\), every \(x\in\mathbb R\) minimizes the penalized objective although only \(0\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distance penalty larger than the global Lipschitz constant is exact; equality at the threshold can leave infeasible minimizers.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and closed}
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Distance-Penalty Threshold

children.title: Projection-Induced Regularizers
children.top_down_role: Regularizer structures whose evaluation or geometry is expressed through set projections.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the squared projection residual, the standard smooth regularizer generated by a closed convex set.

source_refs.locator: 6.3 Prox Calculus Rules p. 135

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), let \(P_Cx\) be the unique minimizer of \(z\mapsto\|x-z\|\) over \(C\). The projection-induced regularizer generated by \(C\) is \[R_C(x):=\frac12\|x-P_Cx\|^2=\frac12\operatorname{dist}(x,C)^2.\] It is finite, convex, and vanishes exactly on \(C\). Moreover, it is Fréchet differentiable on \(H\), with \[\nabla R_C(x)=x-P_Cx.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared distance to a nonempty closed convex set is a finite convex regularizer whose gradient is the residual from the metric projection.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Induced Regularizers

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Prox Calculus Rules p. 135

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact proximal operation for the squared projection-residual regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\gamma>0\) and \(x\in H\), \[\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma R_C}(x)=\frac{x+\gamma P_Cx}{1+\gamma}.\] Thus its evaluation requires one projection onto \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal point is a convex combination of the input and its projection onto the generating set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Representation of Squared Set Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel representation intrinsic to the squared projection-residual regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(R_C(x)=\tfrac12\operatorname{dist}(x,C)^2\), \[R_C=\delta_C\square\tfrac12\|\cdot\|^2,\qquad R_C^*(u)=\sigma_C(u)+\tfrac12\|u\|^2.\] Equivalently, \[R_C(x)=\sup_{u\in H}\{\langle u,x\rangle-\sigma_C(u)-\tfrac12\|u\|^2\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared set distance is a quadratic infimal convolution, and its conjugate is the support function plus the squared norm.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Representation of Squared Set Distance

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projection residual is firmly nonexpansive and one-Lipschitz.

children.title: Projection Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Set geometries governing projection uniqueness, stability, and smoothness of associated distance penalties.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C\) is firmly nonexpansive and \(\nabla(\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,C)^2/2)=I-P_C\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the global convex projection regime from the generally set-valued nonconvex regime.

source_refs.locator: 6.3 Prox Calculus Rules p. 135

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The metric projection is single-valued and firmly nonexpansive: for all \(x,y\in H\), \[\|P_Cx-P_Cy\|^2\leq\langle P_Cx-P_Cy,x-y\rangle.\] Consequently, both \(P_C\) and \(I-P_C\) are nonexpansive, and \(x\mapsto\operatorname{dist}(x,C)^2/2\) is continuously differentiable with gradient \(I-P_C\). If convexity of \(C\) is removed, nearest points may be nonunique, so these global single-valuedness, differentiability, and nonexpansiveness conclusions need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex sets have unique firmly nonexpansive projections and smooth squared-distance regularizers; nonconvex sets can lose all three properties.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Regularity Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Prox Calculus Rules p. 135

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact normal-cone and variational-inequality certificate for projection onto a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be nonempty, closed, and convex in a real Hilbert space. For \(p\in C\), the following are equivalent: \(p=P_Cx\); \(x-p\in N_C(p)\); and \(\langle x-p,y-p\rangle\le0\) for every \(y\in C\). Consequently, \(\|x-y\|^2\ge\|x-p\|^2+\|y-p\|^2\) for every \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is the projection exactly when its residual is normal to the set, yielding the projection Pythagorean inequality.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p=P_Cx\iff x-p\in N_C(p)\iff\langle x-p,y-p\rangle\le0\ \forall y\in C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal example for loss of single-valued projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\{-1,1\}\subset\mathbb R\), the point \(0\) has two nearest points, so the metric projection is set-valued there: \(P_C(0)=\{-1,1\}\). Thus closedness without convexity does not ensure projection uniqueness or differentiability of squared distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed two-point set has a set-valued projection at its midpoint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct claim, but canonically owned by the dedicated nonclosed-set boundary node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=(0,\infty)\subset\mathbb R\) and \(x=0\), one has \(d_C(0)=0\) but no nearest point in \(C\), so \(P_C(0)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed convex set can fail to contain a nearest point.
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Boundary for Projection Attainment

assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Moreau-Rockafellar sum rule with a relative-interior qualification.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.2. Subdifferential Calculus p. 192

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i\), one always has \[\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x)\subseteq\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(x).\] Under the stated relative-interior qualification, the inclusion is exact: \[\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x).\] Here the sum on the right is the Minkowski sum of the component subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgradients of convex summands always add to valid composite subgradients, and a common relative-interior point makes the sum rule exact.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Sum-Rule Family

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Failure of the Unqualified Sum Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indicators whose domains meet without a relative-interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\overline B((0,1),1)\), \(D=\overline B((0,-1),1)\), \(f=\delta_C\), and \(g=\delta_D\). Since \(C\cap D=\{0\}\), \[\partial(f+g)(0)=\mathbb R^2,\] but \[\partial f(0)+\partial g(0)=\{(0,t):t\in\mathbb R\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Indicators of externally tangent disks show strict sum-rule failure without qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) and \(D\) are the displayed tangent disks.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions. If one function is finite and continuous at some point of the other's domain, then for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\), \[\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex subdifferential sum rule is exact when one summand is continuous at a point in the other's domain.
assumptions_latex: One summand is finite and continuous at some point in the domain of the other.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuity-Point Sum-Rule Qualification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-indicator specialization of the finite-dimensional convex sum rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If nonempty convex sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) satisfy \(\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}C_i\ne\varnothing\), then for every \(x\in\bigcap_iC_i\), \[N_{\cap_iC_i}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^mN_{C_i}(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a common relative-interior point, the normal cone to an intersection is the sum of the component normal cones.

children.title: Affine Composition Calculus
children.top_down_role: Subdifferential structures for convex components composed with affine mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(h(x)=g(Ax+b)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex chain rule for an affine inner mapping.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.2. Subdifferential Calculus p. 192

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At every \(x\) with \(Ax+b\in\operatorname{dom}g\), the elementary chain-rule inclusion is \[A^{\mathsf T}\partial g(Ax+b)\subseteq\partial h(x).\] If the affine range meets the relative interior of \(\operatorname{dom}g\), then equality holds at every such \(x\): \[\partial h(x)=\{A^{\mathsf T}v:v\in\partial g(Ax+b)\}.\] Thus every composite subgradient is the pullback by \(A^{\mathsf T}\) of an outer subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a relative-interior qualification, the subdifferential of a convex function composed with an affine map is the adjoint pullback of the outer subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Composition Calculus

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4.2. Subdifferential Calculus p. 192

children.title: Monotone Scalar Composition Calculus
children.top_down_role: Subdifferential structures for scalar outer components with suitable monotonicity.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is finite and convex.
\(J\subset\mathbb R\) is an open interval containing \(f(\mathbb R^n)\).
\(\phi:J\to\mathbb R\) is finite, convex, and nondecreasing.

notation.meaning: scalar multiplier drawn from the outer subdifferential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued scalar outer composition, avoiding extended-value boundary qualifications.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.2. Subdifferential Calculus p. 192

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The composite \(x\mapsto\phi(f(x))\) is finite and convex. For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), its subdifferential is \[\partial(\phi\circ f)(x)=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\partial\phi(f(x))}\alpha\,\partial f(x)=\{\alpha u:\alpha\in\partial\phi(f(x)),\ u\in\partial f(x)\}.\] Nonnegativity of every \(\alpha\in\partial\phi(f(x))\), which follows from monotonicity, is what preserves convexity of the composition and validates the scalar multiplication rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite convex inner function and a convex nondecreasing scalar outer function, composite subgradients are products of compatible outer and inner subgradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Scalar Composition Calculus

children.title: Chain-Rule Qualification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regularity regimes controlling exact versus partial chain-rule descriptions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior Qualification Is Sufficient but Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness can persist for a particular affine composite even when the standard relative-interior condition fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=\delta_{[0,+\infty)}\) and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be the zero map. Then \(A\mathbb R^n=\{0\}\) does not meet \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)=(0,+\infty)\). Nevertheless, \(g\circ A\equiv0\), \(\partial g(0)=(-\infty,0]\), and \[\partial(g\circ A)(x)=\{0\}=A^{\mathsf T}\partial g(0)\quad\text{for every }x.\] Thus the usual relative-interior condition is sufficient for uniform exactness but is not necessary in every instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine chain rule can remain exact even when its standard relative-interior qualification fails.
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is the zero map.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Qualification Is Sufficient but Not Necessary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dropping monotonicity of the scalar outer function can destroy convexity of the composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(\phi(t)=-t\). Both \(f\) and \(\phi\) are convex, but \(\phi\) is decreasing and \[(\phi\circ f)(x)=-x^2\] is not convex. Hence convexity preservation, and therefore the stated convex-subdifferential product rule, does not extend to arbitrary convex outer functions without the required monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex decreasing outer function can turn a convex inner function into a nonconvex composite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\circ f=-x^2\) is not convex, so the monotone scalar convex chain rule is inapplicable.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Failure Without Outer Monotonicity

assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is the zero linear map.

notation.meaning: relative interior of the effective domain

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, but \(\partial g(0)=\varnothing\). Since \(A\mathbb R^n=\{0\}\) does not meet \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)=(0,+\infty)\), the affine qualification fails. Nevertheless, \((g\circ A)(x)=0\) for every \(x\), so \[\partial(g\circ A)(x)=\{0\},\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\partial g(Ax)=A^{\mathsf T}\partial g(0)=\varnothing.\] Hence the unqualified chain-rule inclusion can be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without the affine relative-interior qualification, the composite can have a subgradient even when the outer subdifferential, and therefore its adjoint pullback, is empty.
knowledge_statements.title: Chain-Rule Qualification Boundaries

children.title: Finite-Max Subdifferential Rules
children.top_down_role: Subdifferential calculus for pointwise maxima over finite component families.

assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
All \(f_i\) are finite and continuous at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex maximum at a common continuity point.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.2. Subdifferential Calculus p. 192
3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\) and \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). Then \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right).\] Equivalently, \(v\in\partial f(x)\) exactly when there are coefficients \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and vectors \(v_i\in\partial f_i(x)\), indexed by \(I(x)\), such that \(\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1\) and \(v=\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i v_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient of a finite convex maximum is exactly a convex combination of subgradients belonging to functions active at the evaluation point.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Max Subdifferential Rules

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4.2. Subdifferential Calculus p. 192

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimality Certificate for a Finite Convex Maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained minimization of a finite pointwise maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the finite-max rule, \(x\) minimizes \(f=\max_i f_i\) iff there exist \(\lambda_i\ge0\) and \(v_i\in\partial f_i(x)\), \(i\in I(x)\), such that \[\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1,\qquad\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_iv_i=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point minimizes a finite convex maximum exactly when zero is a convex combination of active component subgradients.
assumptions_latex: The accepted finite-max subdifferential-rule hypotheses hold at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Optimality Certificate for a Finite Convex Maximum

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued finite maximum lacking a common continuity or relative-interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\overline B((0,1),1)\), \(D=\overline B((0,-1),1)\), \(f_1=\delta_C\), and \(f_2=\delta_D\). At \(0\), \(\max(f_1,f_2)=\delta_{\{0\}}\), so \[\partial\max(f_1,f_2)(0)=\mathbb R^2,\] whereas \[\operatorname{conv}(N_C(0)\cup N_D(0))=\{(0,t):t\in\mathbb R\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Indicators of tangent disks show strict failure of the active-subgradient hull formula without qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) and \(D\) are the displayed tangent closed disks.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without a Max-Rule Qualification

children.title: Indexed-Supremum Subdifferential Rules
children.top_down_role: Subdifferential calculus for suprema over infinite or continuously indexed families.

knowledge_statements.title: Indexed-Supremum Subdifferential Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact continuously indexed convex functions on a finite-dimensional open domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a compact topological space and define \(f(z)=\sup_{t\in T}f_t(z)\) for \(z\in U\). Compactness and continuity imply that the supremum is attained, so \(T(x)\neq\varnothing\). At every \(x\in U\), \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{t\in T(x)}\partial f_t(x)\right).\] Thus only active parameters contribute to the subdifferential, with closure retaining limits of convex mixtures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex functions indexed continuously by a compact topological space, the subdifferential of their pointwise supremum is the closed convex hull of subgradients from parameters attaining the supremum.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a compact topological space, and \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open and convex.
For every \(t\in T\), \(f_t:U\to\mathbb R\) is convex.
The mapping \((t,z)\mapsto f_t(z)\) is continuous on \(T\times U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{t\in T(x)}\partial f_t(x)\) for \(f=\sup_{t\in T}f_t\) and every \(x\in U\).

source_refs.locator: 5.4.2. Subdifferential Calculus p. 192

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indexed supremum over a noncompact parameter set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=(0,1)\) and \(f_t(x)=tx\). For \(x>0\), \(f(x)=\sup_{t\in T}tx=x\). Hence \(\partial f(1)=\{1\}\), but \(T(1)=\varnothing\). Exact-active formulas therefore require attainment or replacement by limiting near-active indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supremum can have a nonempty subdifferential even though no parameter attains it.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained Suprema Defeat Active-Parameter Formulas

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-subgradient certificate expressed through epsilon-active indexed components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the hypotheses of the epsilon-active subdifferential formula hold. Then \(x^\star\) minimizes \(f=\sup_{t\in T}f_t\) if and only if \[0\in\bigcap_{\varepsilon>0}\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{t\in T_\varepsilon(x^\star)}\partial_\varepsilon f_t(x^\star)\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point minimizes a finite indexed supremum exactly when zero belongs to every closed epsilon-active epsilon-subgradient hull.
assumptions_latex: \(f_t:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and convex for every \(t\in T\).

notation.meaning: epsilon-active indices at the candidate minimizer

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained-Supremum Optimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued indexed suprema of finite continuous convex functions on Euclidean space, without attainment of the supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{f_t:t\in T\}\) be finite continuous convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\), and suppose \(f:=\sup_{t\in T}f_t\) is finite on \(\mathbb R^n\). For \(\varepsilon>0\), set \(T_\varepsilon(x)=\{t\in T:f_t(x)\ge f(x)-\varepsilon\}\) and \(\partial_\varepsilon f_t(x)=\{u:f_t(y)\ge f_t(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \forall y\}\). Then \[\partial f(x)=\bigcap_{\varepsilon>0}\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{t\in T_\varepsilon(x)}\partial_\varepsilon f_t(x)\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without attained maximizing indices, the subdifferential is recovered from closed convex hulls of epsilon-subgradients of epsilon-active components.
assumptions_latex: \(f_t:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and convex for every \(t\in T\).

children.title: Active-Index Geometry
children.top_down_role: Structural roles of maximizing indices, exposed faces, and active component sets.

assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are finite convex functions for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional and subgradient geometry of a finite convex maximum.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225
5.4.2. Subdifferential Calculus p. 192

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every direction \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), only active components determine the first-order growth of the maximum: \[f'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}f_i'(x;d).\] Since a finite convex function satisfies \(f'(x;d)=\max_{v\in\partial f(x)}\langle v,d\rangle\), the active subdifferentials generate the exposed directional geometry of \(\partial f(x)\). In particular, changing an inactive component without making it active does not change the subdifferential at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a pointwise maximum, active components alone determine every directional derivative and generate the local subdifferential geometry.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Index Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225
5.4.2. Subdifferential Calculus p. 192

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differentiability Criterion for a Finite Convex Maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-index characterization where the finite-max subdifferential rule applies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f=\max_i f_i\) with finite convex \(f_i\), \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) iff \[\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\] is a singleton. Equivalently, every active component is differentiable at \(x\) and all active gradients coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex maximum is differentiable exactly when its active first-order data collapse to one vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ differentiable at }x\iff\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\text{ is a singleton}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Differentiability Criterion for a Finite Convex Maximum

children.title: Marginal-Function Calculus
children.top_down_role: Subdifferential and closure behavior under partial minimization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Joint Function with Nonclosed Marginal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of closedness under finite-dimensional projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(x,y):x>0,\ y\ge1/x\}\) and \(F=\delta_C\). Then \(C\) is closed and convex, but \[p(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)=\delta_{(0,\infty)}(x),\] which is not lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex joint function can have a nonclosed marginal because a closed convex set can have a nonclosed projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is closed convex but \(p=\delta_{(0,\infty)}\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Joint Function with Nonclosed Marginal

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Restriction Formula for Marginal Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional partial minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\) is proper, then \[p^*(u)=F^*(u,0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugating a marginal restricts the joint conjugate to zero dual coordinate for the eliminated variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Restriction Formula for Marginal Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal Closedness Does Not Ensure Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial minimization with an unattained finite infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x,y)=e^y\), \(p(x)=\inf_ye^y=0\) for every \(x\), but \(\operatorname*{argmin}_yF(x,y)=\varnothing\). Thus closedness of \(p\) alone does not permit an attained-minimizer lifting formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A marginal may be finite and closed even though the eliminated-variable infimum is nowhere attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Closedness Does Not Ensure Attainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise subdifferential calculus for an attained partial minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex and let \(p(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\) be proper. If \(y\in\operatorname*{argmin}_zF(x,z)\), then \[u\in\partial p(x)\iff(u,0)\in\partial F(x,y).\] The equivalence holds for every minimizing \(y\) and does not require global closedness of \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an attained partial minimum, marginal subgradients are exactly joint subgradients with zero eliminated-variable component.
knowledge_statements.title: Attained-Marginal Subgradient Lifting

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(p(x)=\inf_y F(x,y)\) is proper, and its local sublevel projections have bounded minimizing variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is closed convex and \(\partial p(x)=\{u:(u,0)\in\partial F(x,y)\}\) for any \(y\in M(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional partial minimization with attainment and level-boundedness ensuring closure.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.2. Subdifferential Calculus p. 192

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partial minimization preserves convexity. Under the stated level-boundedness condition, projection of the relevant epigraphical levels is closed, so \(p\) is also closed and minimizers exist locally. For any \(x\in\operatorname{dom}p\) and any \(y\in M(x)\), \[u\in\partial p(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(u,0)\in\partial F(x,y).\] The right-hand characterization is independent of which minimizing \(y\) is selected. Without a closure or level-boundedness condition, the projected epigraph, and hence the marginal function, need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex function remains convex under partial minimization; with attainment and level-boundedness, the marginal is closed and its subgradients lift with zero eliminated-variable component.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal-Function Calculus

children.title: Fenchel Conjugate Representation
children.top_down_role: Dual descriptions of convex functions through their Fenchel conjugates.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is an extended-real function not identically \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel conjugacy under the Euclidean dual pairing.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Conjugate Calculus Rules p. 91

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Fenchel conjugate of \(f\) is the supremum of affine functions of the dual variable: \[f^*(y):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\}.\] It is convex and lower semicontinuous, regardless of whether \(f\) is convex. For every \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\), Fenchel's inequality holds: \[f(x)+f^*(y)\geq\langle y,x\rangle.\] If \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex, equality is equivalent to \(y\in\partial f(x)\), and also to \(x\in\partial f^*(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel conjugate is the supremum of dual affine minorant gaps; it always satisfies Fenchel's inequality, with equality characterizing paired subgradients for closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel Conjugate Representation

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Conjugate Calculus Rules p. 91

children.title: Biconjugate Closure
children.top_down_role: Closed-convex envelope structure exposed by biconjugation.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and admits an affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}f\), hence \(f=f^{**}\) exactly when \(f\) is lower semicontinuous and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel-Moreau closure correspondence.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Conjugate Calculus Rules p. 91

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[f^{**}(x):=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f^*(y)\}.\] Then \(f^{**}\leq f\), and \(f^{**}\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\). Equivalently, \[f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}f.\] Consequently, a proper function satisfies \(f=f^{**}\) if and only if it is convex and lower semicontinuous. Thus biconjugation removes precisely the nonconvexity and nonclosedness visible to affine minorants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Biconjugation produces the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of a proper function and fixes exactly the closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Biconjugate Closure

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Conjugate Calculus Rules p. 91

children.title: Nonclosed Relaxation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Structural discrepancies between an original function and its closed-convex biconjugate representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indicator Gaps for Nonclosed Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Family of strict biconjugate gaps caused specifically by failure of closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f=\delta_C\). Then \[f^{**}=\delta_{\overline C}.\] Consequently every \(x\in\overline C\setminus C\) satisfies \(f^{**}(x)=0<f(x)=+\infty\). Thus even a proper convex function can differ strictly from its biconjugate when it is not lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of any nonclosed convex set biconjugates to the indicator of its closure, with a strict gap at every missing boundary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{\overline C}\), with strict inequality on \(\overline C\setminus C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Gaps for Nonclosed Convex Sets
Nonclosed Relaxation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary gap between a convex function and its lower-semicontinuous biconjugate relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be the indicator of the open interval \((0,1)\): \(f(x)=0\) for \(0<x<1\) and \(f(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Its Fenchel biconjugate is the indicator of the closed interval: \(f^{**}=\delta_{[0,1]}\). Consequently, at either missing boundary point, \(f^{**}(0)=f^{**}(1)=0\) while \(f(0)=f(1)=+\infty\). Thus biconjugation replaces a nonclosed convex epigraph by its closure and can yield a strict pointwise relaxation gap when lower semicontinuity is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of an open interval becomes the indicator of its closure after biconjugation, producing an infinite-to-zero gap at the endpoints.

notation.meaning: Extended-real indicator of the set C.

children.title: Conjugate Calculus
children.top_down_role: Conjugate transformations of sums, scalings, compositions, and infimal convolutions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Z\) are finite-dimensional real Hilbert spaces.

\(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\neq\varnothing\), and \(\operatorname{range}A\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}h)\neq\varnothing\) for the corresponding minimum formulas.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The four displayed conjugate identities hold, and the two qualified minima are attained.

notation.meaning: Infimal convolution: its value at x is the infimum of f(u)+g(x-u).
Adjoint of the linear map A.
Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on the indicated space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact conjugacy rules under standard relative-interior qualifications.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Conjugate Calculus Rules p. 91

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Z\) be finite-dimensional real Hilbert spaces, let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(X)\), let \(h\in\Gamma_0(Z)\), and let \(\alpha>0\). If \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\neq\varnothing\), then, for every \(y\in X\), \[(f+g)^*(y)=\min_{u\in X}\{f^*(u)+g^*(y-u)\}.\] Moreover, for every \(y\in X\), \[(\alpha f)^*(y)=\alpha f^*(y/\alpha),\qquad (f\mathbin{\square}g)^*(y)=f^*(y)+g^*(y),\] where the second identity applies whenever \(f\mathbin{\square}g\) is proper. If \(A:X\to Z\) is linear and \(\operatorname{range}A\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}h)\neq\varnothing\), then, for every \(y\in X\), \[(h\circ A)^*(y)=\min\{h^*(z):z\in Z,\ A^*z=y\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For functions on explicitly identified finite-dimensional spaces, conjugation converts a qualified sum to infimal convolution, positive scaling to reciprocal argument scaling, a proper infimal convolution to addition, and a qualified linear composition to a constrained conjugate.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Calculus

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Conjugate Calculus Rules p. 91

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate transformations under argument translation and addition of an affine function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, let \(a,c\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\beta\in\mathbb R\). If \(g(x)=f(x-a)+\langle c,x\rangle+\beta\), then \[g^*(y)=f^*(y-c)+\langle y-c,a\rangle-\beta.\] Thus argument translation adds a dual linear term, linear perturbation translates the dual argument, and a constant shift changes the conjugate by the opposite constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Argument translations, linear perturbations, and constant shifts produce an explicit dual translation and affine correction of the conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and extended-real-valued on \(\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: Translated and affinely perturbed version of \(f\).

knowledge_statements.title: Translation and Affine-Perturbation Conjugate Rules

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugation of a coordinatewise separable sum on a product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\) be a finite product of finite-dimensional spaces and let \(f_i:X_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. For \(F(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\), \[F^*(y_1,\ldots,y_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i^*(y_i).\] No relative-interior qualification is needed because the supremum separates over independent coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a coordinatewise separable sum is the sum of the coordinate conjugates.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite product of finite-dimensional spaces.

children.title: Dual-Norm Polarity

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Norm Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar representation of a norm and its dual in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real normed space with dual \(X^*\), pairing \(\langle y,x\rangle\), primal unit ball \(B=\{x:\|x\|\leq1\}\), and polar ball \(B^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in B\}\). Then \(B^\circ\) is the unit ball of the dual norm and
\[\|y\|_*=\sup_{x\in B}\langle y,x\rangle,\qquad \|x\|=\sup_{\|y\|_*\leq1}\langle y,x\rangle.\]
Equivalently, \(\|\cdot\|=\sigma_{B^\circ}\), \(\|\cdot\|_*=\sigma_B\), and \(B^{\circ\circ}=B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each norm is the support function of the other norm's unit ball, and the primal and dual unit balls are mutual polars.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real normed space.

notation.meaning: Polar of the primal unit ball B.
Dual norm induced by the primal norm.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel-polar identity for a finite-dimensional norm and nonnegative scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a norm with dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\), and let \(B_*:=\{y:\|y\|_*\le1\}\). For every \(\lambda\ge0\), \[(\lambda\|\cdot\|)^*=\delta_{\lambda B_*},\qquad \lambda\|x\|=\sigma_{\lambda B_*}(x).\] In particular, at \(\lambda=0\) the conjugate of the zero function is \(\delta_{\{0\}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaled norm and the indicator of the correspondingly scaled dual ball are Fenchel conjugates.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate of a Scaled Norm

children.title: Gauge-Polar Geometry
children.top_down_role: Polar relationships for asymmetric or nonabsorbing gauge constructions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinctions between general gauges and norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\) containing zero, \(\gamma_C\) is sublinear but can be extended-valued when \(C\) is not absorbing. If \(0\ne d\in\operatorname{rec}C\), then \(\gamma_C(d)=0\). Moreover, \(\gamma_C\) is even exactly when its unit set \(C=\{x:\gamma_C(x)\le1\}\) is centrally symmetric; hence a finite positive-definite gauge is a norm exactly when this symmetry holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge may be infinite, vanish in nonzero recession directions, or be asymmetric; central symmetry is the additional condition producing a norm once finiteness and positive definiteness hold.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonabsorption permits \(\gamma_C=+\infty\), recession permits \(\gamma_C(d)=0\) for \(d\ne0\), and evenness is equivalent to central symmetry of C.
knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Degeneracy Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Gauge and Generalized Hölder Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar duality for a compact convex gauge body without symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact and convex with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), and define \(\gamma_C^\circ:=\gamma_{C^\circ}\). Then \[\gamma_C^\circ(y)=\sigma_C(y),\qquad \langle y,x\rangle\le\gamma_C(x)\gamma_C^\circ(y)\quad\forall x,y,\] and \((\gamma_C^\circ)^\circ=\gamma_C\). No central-symmetry assumption is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex body, the polar gauge is the support function of the primal body, satisfies a nonsymmetric Hölder inequality, and recovers the original gauge after polarizing twice.
knowledge_statements.title: Polar Gauge and Generalized Hölder Inequality
Gauge-Polar Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauge representation through the polar set and Fenchel conjugacy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional space with \(0\in C\). Define its gauge by \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\geq0:x\in tC\}\) and its polar by \(C^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}\). Then
\[\gamma_C(x)=\sigma_{C^\circ}(x)=\sup_{y\in C^\circ}\langle y,x\rangle,\qquad \gamma_C^*=\delta_{C^\circ}.\]
If additionally \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), the gauge is finite and continuous everywhere, and \(C=\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set's gauge is the support function of its polar, and its Fenchel conjugate is the polar-set indicator.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains the origin.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gauge-polar identities and the additional interior conclusion are mathematically correct and fit the duality leaf, but no authoritative source locator is supplied.

children.title: Support-Function Polarity
children.top_down_role: Support-function descriptions associated with convex sets and their polar objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support functions as gauges and conjugates of closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional space with \(0\in C\). Its support function is \(\sigma_C(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\), and its polar satisfies
\[C^\circ=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\leq1\}.\]
Moreover,
\[\sigma_C=\delta_C^*,\qquad \sigma_C^*=\delta_C,\qquad \sigma_C=\gamma_{C^\circ}.\]
Thus the closed convex set is recoverable from its support function by \(C=\{x:\langle y,x\rangle\leq\sigma_C(y)\ \forall y\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set's support function is its indicator's conjugate, is the gauge of its polar, and uniquely determines the original set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Mapping Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Firm nonexpansiveness, fixed points, and stability of convex proximal mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), and let \(\lambda>0\). The proximal map \(P=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\) is single-valued and firmly nonexpansive:
\[\|P x-P y\|^2\leq\langle P x-P y,x-y\rangle\quad\forall x,y\in H.\]
Consequently, \(P\) is nonexpansive, \(I-P\) is firmly nonexpansive, and
\[\operatorname{Fix}P=\operatorname*{argmin}f.\]
In particular, perturbing the input by \(x-y\) changes the proximal point by at most \(\|x-y\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex proximal map is single-valued and firmly nonexpansive; its fixed points are exactly the minimizers of the function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\) is firmly nonexpansive and \(\operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f})=\operatorname*{argmin}f\).

notation.meaning: Minimizer of f(u)+(2λ)^{-1} times the squared distance from u to the input.
Set of fixed points of P.
Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on H.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp stability improvement under strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\) is \(\sigma\)-strongly convex with \(\sigma>0\), then for every \(\lambda>0\), \[\|\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(y)\|\leq\frac{1}{1+\lambda\sigma}\|x-y\|.\] The factor is attained for \(f(x)=\tfrac\sigma2\|x\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity improves nonexpansiveness to a sharp contraction with factor one over one plus lambda sigma.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Convexity Contraction of Proximal Maps

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional converse distinguishing proximal mappings from general firmly nonexpansive mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mapping \(T:H\to H\) is \(\operatorname{prox}_f\) for some \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\) if and only if \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive and cyclically monotone. Equivalently, \(T=\nabla\Phi\) for a differentiable convex function \(\Phi\) whose gradient is firmly nonexpansive. The representing \(f\) is unique up to an additive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Firm nonexpansiveness characterizes resolvents; cyclic monotonicity is the additional condition making the resolvent a convex proximal mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T=\operatorname{prox}_f\text{ for some }f\in\Gamma_0(H)\iff T\text{ is firmly nonexpansive and cyclically monotone}.
knowledge_statements.title: Characterization of Convex Proximal Mappings

children.title: Resolvent Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Operator representation of proximal mappings through subdifferentials.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal maps represented as resolvents of convex subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), and \(\lambda>0\). For every \(x\in H\), a point \(p\) satisfies
\[p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\]
if and only if
\[0\in\partial f(p)+\lambda^{-1}(p-x),\]
or equivalently \(x\in p+\lambda\partial f(p)\). Hence
\[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}=(I+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}.\]
Because \(\partial f\) is maximally monotone, this resolvent is defined and single-valued on all of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal map of a closed convex function equals the resolvent of its scaled subdifferential, as follows from the proximal optimality condition.

children.title: Moreau Envelope Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric and regularity properties of proximal envelope representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Moreau Envelope Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smoothness and gradient representation of the convex Moreau envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), and \(\lambda>0\). Define
\[e_\lambda f(x)=\min_u\left\{f(u)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|u-x\|^2\right\}.\]
The minimum is uniquely attained at \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\). The envelope is finite, convex, and continuously differentiable on \(H\), with
\[\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=\lambda^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\bigr).\]
Its gradient is \(1/\lambda\)-Lipschitz and satisfies \(e_\lambda f(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Moreau envelope is a finite smooth convex minorant whose gradient is the scaled residual between a point and its proximal image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_\lambda f\) is convex and differentiable, with \(\nabla e_\lambda f=\lambda^{-1}(I-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f})\) and \(1/\lambda\)-Lipschitz gradient.

notation.meaning: Moreau envelope of f with parameter λ.

source_refs.locator: 6.7 The Moreau Envelope p. 163

source_witnesses.locator: 6.7 The Moreau Envelope p. 163

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Representation of the Moreau Envelope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal infimal-convolution and dual quadratic-regularization representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\). For \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\) and \(\lambda>0\), \[e_\lambda f=f\mathbin{\square}(\lambda^{-1}q)=\bigl(f^*+\lambda q\bigr)^*,\qquad (e_\lambda f)^*=f^*+\lambda q.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moreau regularization is quadratic infimal convolution in the primal and addition of a quadratic term to the conjugate in the dual.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Representation of the Moreau Envelope

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), \(f^*\) its Fenchel conjugate, and \(\lambda>0\). For every \(x\in H\), \[x=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)+\lambda\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\lambda}(x/\lambda).\] The corresponding envelope identity is \[e_\lambda f(x)+e_{1/\lambda}f^*(x/\lambda)=\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x\|^2.\] Thus the primal proximal component and the scaled dual proximal component decompose the identity, while the corresponding envelopes partition the quadratic energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point decomposes into primal and scaled dual proximal components, while the corresponding Moreau envelopes sum to a quadratic energy.
knowledge_statements.title: Moreau Conjugate Decomposition

children.title: Envelope Parameter Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Parameter Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity and limiting regimes of the Moreau smoothing parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\) on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space and assume \(m=\inf_H f> -\infty\). For \(0<\lambda<\mu\),
\[m\leq e_\mu f(x)\leq e_\lambda f(x)\leq f(x)\quad\forall x\in H.\]
For every \(x\in H\), lower semicontinuity gives
\[\lim_{\lambda\downarrow0}e_\lambda f(x)=f(x),\qquad \lim_{\lambda\to\infty}e_\lambda f(x)=m.\]
Thus small parameters recover the original function pointwise, whereas large parameters flatten the envelope toward the optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moreau envelopes decrease as the smoothing parameter grows, converge to the original function at zero, and flatten to the infimum at infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_\mu f\leq e_\lambda f\leq f\) for \(0<\lambda<\mu\), with the displayed pointwise limits.

source_refs.locator: 6.7 The Moreau Envelope p. 163

source_witnesses.locator: 6.7 The Moreau Envelope p. 163

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative effect of the envelope scale on curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\) is \(\sigma\)-strongly convex with \(\sigma>0\), then for every \(\lambda>0\), \(e_\lambda f\) is \(\sigma/(1+\lambda\sigma)\)-strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moreau smoothing changes a strong-convexity modulus from sigma to sigma divided by one plus lambda sigma.

notation.meaning: Strong-convexity modulus of the original function.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Convexity Transformation Across Scale

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition rule for successive positive smoothing scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\) and \(\lambda,\mu>0\), \[e_\mu(e_\lambda f)=e_{\lambda+\mu}f.\] Thus successive quadratic regularizations combine by addition of their scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive Moreau regularizations are equivalent to one regularization at the sum of their parameters.
knowledge_statements.title: Moreau Envelope Semigroup Law

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hamilton–Jacobi Evolution in the Envelope Scale
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential law governing positive-scale Moreau regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), every \(x\in H\), and \(\lambda>0\), \[\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}e_\lambda f(x)=-\frac12\|\nabla e_\lambda f(x)\|^2=-\frac{1}{2\lambda^2}\|x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The envelope's rate of decrease with scale is minus one half of its squared gradient norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Hamilton–Jacobi Evolution in the Envelope Scale

children.title: Proximal Average
children.top_down_role: Interpolation of convex functions through proximal structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugacy with reciprocal scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the seed normalization, \[\bigl(\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_1,\ldots,f_m;w)\bigr)^*=\operatorname{pav}_{1/\mu}(f_1^*,\ldots,f_m^*;w).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel conjugation commutes with proximal averaging after reciprocating the scale.
assumptions_latex: The same quadratic normalization is used on both sides.
knowledge_statements.title: Self-Duality of the Proximal Average

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Location between the epigraphical and arithmetic averages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p=\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_1,\ldots,f_m;w)\), \[\left(\sum_iw_if_i^*\right)^*\leq p\leq\sum_iw_if_i.\] If \(f_i=f\) for every \(i\), then \(p=f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal average lies between the conjugate-based epigraphical average and the ordinary weighted arithmetic average, and identical inputs are reproduced.
knowledge_statements.title: Order Bounds and Idempotence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal Mapping of the Proximal Average
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact weighted averaging identity at the defining scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p=\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_1,\ldots,f_m;w)\), then \[\operatorname{prox}_{\mu p}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\operatorname{prox}_{\mu f_i}(x)\quad\forall x\in H.\] Equivalently, \(\nabla e_\mu p=\sum_iw_i\nabla e_\mu f_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the defining scale, the proximal map of the proximal average is the weighted arithmetic average of the component proximal maps.
assumptions_latex: The proximal-average normalization is the one used in the seed.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Mapping of the Proximal Average

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infimal Representation of the Proximal Average
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space formula displaying the quadratic disagreement penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p=\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_1,\ldots,f_m;w)\) under the seed convention. Then \[p(x)=\inf_{\sum_iw_ix_i=x}\left\{\sum_iw_if_i(x_i)+\frac{1}{2\mu}\left(\sum_iw_i\|x_i\|^2-\|x\|^2\right)\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal average minimizes the weighted component values plus a quadratic penalty for disagreement among component points with prescribed weighted mean.
knowledge_statements.title: Infimal Representation of the Proximal Average
Proximal Average
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted interpolation of closed convex functions preserving Moreau-envelope structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\Gamma_0(H)\), let \(w_i>0\) satisfy \(\sum_iw_i=1\), and let \(\mu>0\). With \(q(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), define the proximal average by
\[\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_1,\ldots,f_m;w)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\left(f_i+\mu^{-1}q\right)^*\right)^*-\mu^{-1}q.\]
This function belongs to \(\Gamma_0(H)\) and is characterized by
\[e_\mu\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_1,\ldots,f_m;w)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i e_\mu f_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal average conjugates a weighted sum of quadratically regularized conjugates and has a Moreau envelope equal to the weighted average of the input envelopes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed formula defines an element of \(\Gamma_0(H)\) whose \(\mu\)-Moreau envelope is \(\sum_iw_i e_\mu f_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and envelope characterization are standard and fit the Proximal Average container, but the record supplies no authoritative source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugacy, Envelope, and Proximity Identities for the Proximal Average
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the principal closure and averaging identities for the equally weighted proximal average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) and \(q=\tfrac12\lVert\cdot\rVert^2\). Then
\[
\operatorname{pav}(f,g)\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H),\qquad
\bigl(\operatorname{pav}(f,g)\bigr)^*=\operatorname{pav}(f^*,g^*),
\]
\[
\operatorname{pav}(f,g)\square q=\frac12(f\square q)+\frac12(g\square q),
\qquad
\operatorname{Prox}_{\operatorname{pav}(f,g)}=\frac12\operatorname{Prox}_f+\frac12\operatorname{Prox}_g.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal average of two proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions remains in the same class. Conjugation commutes with proximal averaging; its quadratic infimal convolution is the arithmetic mean of the two individual quadratic infimal convolutions; and its proximity operator is the arithmetic mean of the two individual proximity operators.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal Average of Two Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the equally weighted proximal average on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\). Their proximal average is the extended-real-valued function \(\operatorname{pav}(f,g):\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) defined by
\[
\operatorname{pav}(f,g)(x)=\frac12\inf_{\substack{(y,z)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\\y+z=2x}}\left(f(y)+g(z)+\frac14\lVert y-z\rVert^2\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions f and g on a Hilbert space, their equally weighted proximal average at x is one half of the infimum of f(y)+g(z) plus one quarter of the squared distance between y and z, over all y and z whose sum is 2x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Bounds for the Proximal Average
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Places the proximal average between the conjugate harmonic-type mean and the arithmetic mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), the following pointwise inequalities hold on \(\mathcal H\):

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Structural Properties of the Proximal Average
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records symmetry, an infimal-postcomposition representation, the exact effective domain, and proper convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), define \(L:\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) by \(L(y,z)=(y+z)/2\), and define
\[
F(y,z)=\frac12f(y)+\frac12g(z)+\frac18\lVert y-z\rVert^2.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{pav}(f,g)=\operatorname{pav}(g,f)=L\mathbin{\triangleright}F,
\qquad
\operatorname{dom}\operatorname{pav}(f,g)=\frac12\operatorname{dom}f+\frac12\operatorname{dom}g,
\]
and \(\operatorname{pav}(f,g)\) is proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal average is symmetric. It is the infimal postcomposition of the specified product-space function F by the averaging map L, its domain is exactly the half-scaled Minkowski sum of the domains of f and g, and it is a proper convex function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Support Representation of the Closed Perspective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel representation of a closed convex perspective as a support function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(\widetilde f\) be its closed perspective, and define \[K_f:=\{(y,\eta):f^*(y)+\eta\le0\}.\] Then \[\widetilde f(x,t)=\sigma_{K_f}(x,t).\] For \(t>0\), this equals \(\sup_y\{\langle y,x\rangle-tf^*(y)\}\); at \(t=0\) it equals \(f^\infty(x)\), and for \(t<0\) it is \(+\infty\). Consequently \(\widetilde f^*=\delta_{K_f}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective is the support function of the set determined by the conjugate, and its conjugate is that set's indicator.
assumptions_latex: \(\widetilde f\) uses the recession value at zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Support Representation of the Closed Perspective
Perspective Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed homogeneous perspective of an extended-real convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex. Its closed perspective is the function \(\widetilde f:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) defined by
\[\widetilde f(x,t)=\begin{cases}t f(x/t),&t>0,\\ f^\infty(x),&t=0,\\ +\infty,&t<0,\end{cases}\]
where \(f^\infty\) is the recession function. Then \(\widetilde f\) is proper, closed, convex, and positively homogeneous: \(\widetilde f(\alpha x,\alpha t)=\alpha\widetilde f(x,t)\) for every \(\alpha\geq0\). Its epigraph is the closure of the conic hull of \(\{(x,1,r):f(x)\leq r\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective homogenizes a convex function, using its recession function at zero, and converts its epigraph into a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde f\) is proper, closed, convex, positively homogeneous, and has the displayed conic epigraph representation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed-perspective definition, recession value at zero, homogeneity, and conic epigraph representation fit the container, but no authoritative source locator is supplied.

children.title: Epigraphical Lifts
children.top_down_role: Lifted representations for maxima, norms, and structured penalties.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact epigraph lifting for finite structured sums, maxima, and norm penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(A_i:X\to Y_i\) be affine, and let \(r_i:Y_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Whenever the displayed extended-real sums are well-defined, \[\inf_x\left(F(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(A_i x)\right)=\inf_{x,t_1,\ldots,t_m}\left\{F(x)+\sum_i t_i:(A_i x,t_i)\in\operatorname{epi}r_i\ \forall i\right\}.\] Eliminating \(t_i\) recovers each objective value. For \(r=\max_i r_i\), one epigraph variable satisfies \(r_i(Ax)\le t\) for every i; for \(r(y)=\|y\|\), it satisfies \(\|Ax\|\le t\). Whenever minimizers exist, projection of lifted minimizers gives exactly the original minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structured sums, finite maxima, and norm penalties admit exact auxiliary epigraph formulations that preserve objective values and minimizers under projection.
assumptions_latex: The displayed extended-real sums are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eliminating the epigraph variables recovers the original objective pointwise and preserves its infimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Epigraphical Lifts
Epigraphical Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional epigraph lifts for composite penalties, maxima, and norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(F:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), let \(A:X\to Y\) be affine, and let \(r:Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper. Then
\[
\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(F(x)+r(Ax)\bigr)=\inf_{x\in X,\,t\in\mathbb R}\{F(x)+t:(Ax,t)\in\operatorname{epi}r\}.
\]
If \(r(y)=\max_{1\le i\le m}r_i(y)\), the epigraph condition is equivalent to \(r_i(Ax)\le t\) for every \(i\). If \(r(y)=\lVert y\rVert\), it becomes \(\lVert Ax\rVert\le t\). If the common infimum is finite and attained, projection onto \(x\) maps the lifted minimizers exactly onto the original minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite penalty can be replaced by an auxiliary epigraph variable; maxima become simultaneous inequalities and norms become norm-cone constraints. Optimal values are unchanged, and when the common finite optimum is attained, the original-variable minimizers are preserved under lifting and projection.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(A:X\to Y\) is affine and \(F,r\) are extended-real-valued functions.
The displayed problems are interpreted using the same extended-real conventions.
