children.title: Analytic Applicability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failures affecting meaningful objective values, attainment, exact calculus, or dual representation.

children.title: Component Properness-Closure Failures
children.top_down_role: Component defects affecting closure and value behavior.

children.title: Improper Components
children.top_down_role: Component pathologies involving improper extended-value structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Properness Test for a Finite Component Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain-compatibility criterion for sums of proper extended-real convex components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(i=1,\ldots,k\), be proper extended-real convex functions. Then \(H=\sum_{i=1}^k h_i\) never takes \(-\infty\), and \[H\text{ is proper}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\bigcap_{i=1}^k\operatorname{dom}h_i\ne\varnothing.\] Thus separately proper components may form an identically-positive-infinite composite when their effective domains have empty intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sum of proper convex components is proper exactly when their effective domains share a point.
assumptions_latex: Every \(h_i\) is proper and extended-real convex.

notation.meaning: finite pointwise sum of the components

knowledge_statements.title: Properness Test for a Finite Component Sum

assumptions_latex: \(h:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex in the extended-real sense.
A composite model uses \(h\) as an objective component.
Standard subdifferential or conjugacy rules under consideration require proper components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(h\equiv+\infty\) or \(h(x)=-\infty\) somewhere, proper-component calculus and its optimality certificates are inapplicable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of standard composite calculus when an extended-real component is not proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The component \(h\) is proper when \(h(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(\operatorname{dom}h=\{x:h(x)<+\infty\}\neq\varnothing\). It is improper if either \(h\equiv+\infty\) or \(h(x)=-\infty\) for some \(x\). In the first case, any sum containing \(h\) is identically \(+\infty\) unless undefined extended-real arithmetic intervenes; in the second, the usual proper convex conjugacy and subdifferential framework does not apply. Consequently, composite optimality, duality, and proximal statements whose hypotheses require proper components cannot be invoked until properness is restored or a separate extended-value convention is justified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A component is improper if its finite domain is empty or it takes minus infinity; standard composite subdifferential and duality certificates then do not apply.
knowledge_statements.title: Improper Components

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The properness boundary is correctly characterized and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Nonclosed Components
children.top_down_role: Component pathologies involving failure of closedness.

assumptions_latex: Closedness means lower semicontinuity, equivalently a closed epigraph in finite dimensions.
The closure \(\operatorname{cl}h\) denotes the lower-semicontinuous convex hull represented by the epigraph closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity alone does not ensure closedness, and replacing a nonclosed component by its closure can add boundary points to its domain.

notation.meaning: indicator function of a set S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary failure for a proper convex but nonclosed component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[h(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x>0,\\+\infty,&x\leq0.\end{cases}\]
This function is proper and convex, but it is not closed because \(x_k\downarrow0\) gives \(h(x_k)=0\) while \(h(0)=+\infty\). Its epigraph closure yields
\[(\operatorname{cl}h)(x)=\delta_{[0,\infty)}(x),\]
so \((\operatorname{cl}h)(0)=0<h(0)\). Therefore results requiring a closed component cannot be applied to \(h\) merely from convexity and properness. Replacing \(h\) by \(\operatorname{cl}h\) repairs closedness but changes the boundary domain and may change the composite problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function may exclude a finite boundary limit. Closing it adds that boundary value and can alter the composite model.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Components

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example is a valid proper convex nonclosed component and its closure is correctly identified, but the record lacks cited evidence.

children.title: Closure-Induced Value Changes
children.top_down_role: Value behavior altered by closure or lower-semicontinuous regularization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General value ordering after selected components are replaced by their lower-semicontinuous convex closures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_1,\ldots,h_k:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be extended-real convex functions with proper lower-semicontinuous convex closures. Since \(\operatorname{cl}h_i\le h_i\) pointwise, replacing components indexed by \(I\) gives \[\inf_x\left(\sum_{i\in I}(\operatorname{cl}h_i)(x)+\sum_{i\notin I}h_i(x)\right)\le \inf_x\sum_{i=1}^k h_i(x).\] Equality is not automatic because closure may add boundary points compatible with the remaining components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing components can only lower the composite objective pointwise and may strictly lower its optimal value by adding compatible boundary points.
assumptions_latex: Every closure used in the replacement is proper.
The displayed sums avoid indeterminate extended-real arithmetic.

notation.meaning: lower-semicontinuous convex closure of component i
indices of components replaced by their closures

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Closure Is a Relaxation

assumptions_latex: Closure is taken in the lower-semicontinuous convex sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original composite value is \(+\infty\), whereas replacing \(h\) by \(\operatorname{cl}h\) changes it to \(0\).

notation.meaning: indicator function of a set S
indicator of the open positive ray

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample showing that component closure can change a composite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h(x)=\delta_{(0,\infty)}(x)\) and \(q(x)=\delta_{\{0\}}(x)\). Their domains are disjoint, so
\[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\bigl(h(x)+q(x)\bigr)=+\infty.\]
The lower-semicontinuous closure of \(h\) is \(\operatorname{cl}h=\delta_{[0,\infty)}\). After replacing only this component by its closure, the point \(x=0\) belongs to both effective domains and
\[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\bigl((\operatorname{cl}h)(x)+q(x)\bigr)=0.\]
Thus componentwise closure is not an innocuous analytic normalization: at a boundary enforced by another component, it can change the composite optimal value from \(+\infty\) to a finite value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing an open-domain indicator before adding a boundary constraint changes the composite value from infeasible to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Induced Value Changes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly shows that componentwise closure changes the composite value from positive infinity to zero, but no source or locator supports it.

children.title: Recession-Driven Nonattainment
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic structures preventing attained solutions.

children.title: Primal Nonattainment
children.top_down_role: Finite or limiting optimal values lacking attained primal solutions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Level-Bounded Lower-Semicontinuous Objectives Attain Their Infima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional condition excluding primal nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. If every sublevel set of \(F\) is bounded, then \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}F(x)\ne\varnothing.\] Consequently, a proper lower-semicontinuous objective with finite unattained infimum is not level-bounded. Convexity is unnecessary for this implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, proper lower semicontinuity and bounded sublevels guarantee a minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper and lower semicontinuous on \(\mathbb R^n\).
Every sublevel set of \(F\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Bounded Lower-Semicontinuous Objectives Attain Their Infima

assumptions_latex: The objective is the proper closed convex function \(F(x)=e^x\).
No compactness, level-boundedness, or other attainment hypothesis is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite infimum \(0\) is not attained, and minimizing sequences escape along the recession direction \(-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional recession-driven failure of primal attainment despite closed convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x)=e^x\), one has \(F(x)>0\) for every finite \(x\), while the sequence \(x_k=-k\) satisfies \(F(x_k)=e^{-k}\to0\). Hence
\[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}F(x)=0,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}}F(x)=\varnothing.\]
The direction \(d=-1\) has zero recession cost, \(F^\infty(d)=0\), and the minimizing sequence escapes to infinity along this direction. Thus properness, closedness, convexity, and finiteness of the infimum do not ensure primal attainment; an additional condition such as level-boundedness, compact feasible level sets, or a suitable recession exclusion is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex function exp(x) has infimum zero but no minimizer; minimizing sequences escape toward minus infinity along a zero-cost recession direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Nonattainment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponential example correctly demonstrates primal nonattainment and zero recession cost in direction -1, and the counterexample kind fits the leaf. It nevertheless lacks a source and locator.

children.title: Adverse Recession Directions
children.top_down_role: Recession structures that obstruct bounded or attained solution behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^\infty(d)<0\Rightarrow\inf F=-\infty\), while \(F^\infty(d)=0\) identifies a direction along which bounded sublevel sets may fail.

notation.meaning: Recession function of the composite objective

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional recession criterion for a closed convex composite objective.

source_refs.locator: 1.4.1. Directions of Recession of a Convex Function p. 50

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The recession function is \[F^\infty(d)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}F}\bigl(F(x+d)-F(x)\bigr).\] A nonzero vector \(d\) is adverse when \(F^\infty(d)\leq 0\). If \(F^\infty(d)<0\), then for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\), the values \(F(x+td)\) tend to \(-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\). If \(F^\infty(d)=0\), objective values need not decrease strictly, but sublevel sets may be unbounded in direction \(d\), so compactness-based attainment arguments do not apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction with negative recession value makes the objective unbounded below; a zero-recession direction can destroy boundedness needed for attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Adverse Recession Directions

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4.1. Directions of Recession of a Convex Function p. 50

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional exclusion of adverse recession directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex. Then \[F\text{ is level-bounded}\iff F^\infty(d)>0\quad\text{for every }d\ne0.\] Hence failure of level-boundedness is equivalent to existence of a nonzero \(d\) with \(F^\infty(d)\le0\). If \(F\) is bounded below, every such adverse direction has \(F^\infty(d)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex objective has bounded sublevels exactly when every nonzero direction has positive recession cost.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Boundedness Characterized by Recession Growth

children.title: Infimal Escape Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where minimizing sequences escape while approaching the infimum.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every sequence \((x_k)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(F(x_k)\to p\) obeys \(\lVert x_k\rVert_2\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional escape property for minimizing sequences associated with an unattained finite infimum.

source_refs.locator: 1.4.1. Directions of Recession of a Convex Function p. 50

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An infimal escape regime occurs when \(p=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}F(x)\in\mathbb{R}\), the value \(p\) is not attained, and \((x_k)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \(F(x_k)\to p\). For every such minimizing sequence, \(\lVert x_k\rVert_2\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-semicontinuous finite-dimensional objective, every minimizing sequence escapes to infinity when the finite infimum is unattained.
knowledge_statements.title: Infimal Escape Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4.1. Directions of Recession of a Convex Function p. 50

children.title: Failed Calculus Qualification
children.top_down_role: Loss of exact additive, chain, marginal, or conjugate calculus.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of closed marginal calculus under unconstrained projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(x,y):x>0,\ y\ge1/x\}\) and \(H=\delta_C\). Although \(C\) is closed and convex, \[p(x)=\inf_y H(x,y)=\delta_{(0,\infty)}(x),\] which is convex but not lower semicontinuous. Thus projection of a closed convex epigraph need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex integrand can have a nonclosed marginal because projection need not preserve closedness.
assumptions_latex: \(H=\delta_C\) for the stated closed convex set.
No compactness or closed-projection condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p=\delta_{(0,\infty)}\text{ is convex but not closed}.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Convex Marginal

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of an exact minimizing representative in an eliminated variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(H(x,y)=e^y\), the marginal satisfies \[p(x)=\inf_y H(x,y)=0\qquad(x\in\mathbb R),\] but no finite \(y\) attains the infimum. Thus a finite closed convex marginal need not possess an attaining eliminated variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite closed convex marginal can be defined by an unattained infimum.
assumptions_latex: The variable y is eliminated by unconstrained infimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Infimum Without Attainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of exact adjoint-pullback calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(u,v):v\ge u^2\}\), \(g=\delta_C\), and \(Ax=(x,0)\). Then \(g\circ A=\delta_{\{0\}}\), so \(\partial(g\circ A)(0)=\mathbb R\). By contrast, \(N_C(0,0)=\{(0,\beta):\beta\le0\}\), hence \[A^*\partial g(A0)=\{0\}\subsetneq\partial(g\circ A)(0).\] Here \(\operatorname{range}A\cap\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the range misses the relative interior of the outer domain, the affine-chain inclusion can be strict.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Chain-Rule Failure Without Qualification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of exact additive subdifferential calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(u,v):v\ge u^2\}\), \(D=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\), \(f=\delta_C\), and \(g=\delta_D\). Then \(C\cap D=\{(0,0)\}\), so \(\partial(f+g)(0,0)=\mathbb R^2\). However, \(\partial f(0,0)=\{(0,\beta):\beta\le0\}\) and \(\partial g(0,0)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\), whence \[\partial f(0,0)+\partial g(0,0)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\subsetneq\mathbb R^2.\] The relative interiors of the two domains do not intersect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangent convex domains can make the unconditional subdifferential sum inclusion strict.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are indicators of the stated nonempty closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Sum Rule Without Qualification

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a qualification such as \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\neq\varnothing\), exact sum and conjugate calculus is not guaranteed.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for exact finite-dimensional convex sum and conjugate rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inclusion \[\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\subseteq\partial(f+g)(x)\] always holds, but equality is not ensured when the relative-interior qualification \[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\neq\varnothing\] is unavailable. Correspondingly, the identity \[(f+g)^*(y)=\inf_{u+v=y}\bigl(f^*(u)+g^*(v)\bigr)\] may require lower-semicontinuous closure, and the displayed infimum may fail to be attained. Failure of the qualification removes these guarantees; it does not by itself imply that every equality fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a relative-interior qualification, exact subdifferential and conjugate sum rules may become strict, require closure, or lose attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Failed Calculus Qualification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary formulation is mathematically plausible and correctly avoids claiming that qualification failure forces calculus failure. However, the exact subdifferential and conjugate-calculus assertions have no inspectable citation, so source support is required.

children.title: Dual Certification Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Failure of intended primal-dual representation or certification.

children.title: Positive Duality Gaps
children.top_down_role: Regimes where intended primal and dual values fail to coincide.

assumptions_latex: The primal and dual optimal values are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A positive duality gap is the strict inequality \(p^*>d^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel composite primal-dual value gap.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2. General Optimization Duality p. 138

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal problem and its Fenchel dual, define \[p^*=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl(f(x)+g(Ax)\bigr),\qquad d^*=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\bigl(-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\bigr).\] Weak duality gives \(d^*\leq p^*\). When both values are finite, a positive duality gap is the strict inequality \[p^*-d^*>0.\] In this regime no primal-dual pair can satisfy an exact zero-gap optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive duality gap occurs when the finite Fenchel primal value strictly exceeds the finite dual value.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Duality Gaps

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.2. General Optimization Duality p. 138

children.title: Dual Nonattainment
children.top_down_role: Regimes where the dual value lacks an attaining dual solution.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual nonattainment means that \(D(y)<d^*\) for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(D(y)>-\infty\), although there is a sequence \((y_k)\) of such points with \(D(y_k)\to d^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonattainment of a finite Fenchel-dual supremum.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2. General Optimization Duality p. 138
5.3.4. Duality and Existence of Optimal Primal Solutions p. 176

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[D(y)=-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y),\qquad d^*=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}D(y),\] and suppose \(d^*\in\mathbb{R}\). A point \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) is dual feasible when \(D(y)>-\infty\). Dual nonattainment occurs when \(D(y)<d^*\) for every dual-feasible \(y\), while a sequence \((y_k)\) of dual-feasible points satisfies \(D(y_k)\to d^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite Fenchel-dual value is approached by dual-feasible sequences but is realized by no dual-feasible point.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Nonattainment

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.2. General Optimization Duality p. 138
5.3.4. Duality and Existence of Optimal Primal Solutions p. 176

children.title: Primal–Dual Certificate Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Loss or weakening of certificates caused by duality pathologies.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, convex functions and \(A\) is linear.
\(x\) and \(y\) are primal and dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inclusions \(-A^*y\in\partial f(x)\) and \(y\in\partial g(Ax)\) certify zero gap; positive gap or missing dual attainment precludes such an exact pair.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Fenchel primal-dual subgradient certificate and its breakdown.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191
4.2.2. General Optimization Duality p. 138

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal objective \(f(x)+g(Ax)\), an exact certificate is a pair \((x,y)\) satisfying \[-A^*y\in\partial f(x),\qquad y\in\partial g(Ax).\] Fenchel-Young equality then gives \[f(x)+g(Ax)=-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y),\] certifying primal and dual optimality with zero gap. If the optimal values have a positive gap, no such pair exists. If the dual supremum is not attained, no exact certificate with a dual optimizer exists, even when the primal value equals the dual supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matching primal and dual subgradients certify optimality and zero gap; positive gaps or dual nonattainment destroy this exact certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Certificate Breakdown

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191
4.2.2. General Optimization Duality p. 138

children.title: Computational Applicability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where formal component structure does not yield a useful computational interface.

children.title: Nondecomposable Proximal Maps
children.top_down_role: Sums or compositions whose proximal maps do not inherit componentwise simplicity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical sufficient structure under which a proximal mapping decomposes componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb R^n=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_q\) be an orthogonal direct sum, let \(P_i\) be the orthogonal projection onto \(H_i\), and let \(f_i:H_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex. For
\[F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^q f_i(P_i x),\]
one has for every \(\lambda>0\),
\[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}(z)=\sum_{i=1}^q\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f_i}(P_i z).\]
Thus decomposition follows from orthogonal variable-block separability, not from an arbitrary additive expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A summed proximal map decomposes across orthogonal variable blocks; an arbitrary coupled sum does not.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb R^n\) is the orthogonal direct sum of the subspaces \(H_i\).
Each \(f_i\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(H_i\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal direct-sum decomposition of the variable space

knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonal Block Separability Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(\delta_C\) denotes the indicator of a set \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In general, \(\operatorname{prox}_{\delta_U+\delta_V}\neq P_U P_V\), so proximal maps of sums do not decompose by composing component proximal maps.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of componentwise proximal composition for a sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=\{(s,0):s\in\mathbb{R}\}\), \(V=\{(s,s):s\in\mathbb{R}\}\), and \(z=(1,0)\). Since \(U\cap V=\{0\}\), \[\operatorname{prox}_{\delta_U+\delta_V}(z)=P_{U\cap V}z=(0,0).\] However, \[P_UP_Vz=P_U(1/2,1/2)=(1/2,0).\] Thus the proximal map of a sum cannot generally be evaluated by sequentially applying the component proximal maps, even though each component is individually easy to evaluate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two simple projection proximal maps need not compose to the proximal map of their summed indicator functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Nondecomposable Proximal Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection counterexample is internally correct and fits the nondecomposable-proximal-map leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation beyond a standard-field flag. An authoritative proximal-calculus source is required.

children.title: General Transform Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Linear or nonlinear compositions that destroy direct evaluation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical exception to the failure of direct proximal evaluation through a linear transform.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R^m\) be linear with \(AA^	op=
u I_m\) for some \(
u>0\), and let \(g:\mathbb R^m	o(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex. For every \(\lambda>0\),
\[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda(g\circ A)}(z)=z+
u^{-1}A^	op igl(\operatorname{prox}_{
u\lambda g}(Az)-Az igr).\]
Thus the direct formula holds under scaled coisometry; invertibility alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear composition has a direct proximal formula when the transform has orthogonal rows up to a common scale; invertibility alone does not suffice.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is linear and \(AA^\top=\nu I_m\) for some \(\nu>0\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean proximal mapping of the scaled function

knowledge_statements.title: Tight-Transform Proximal Formula

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identity \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda(g\circ A)}(z)=A^{-1}\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(Az)\) fails in general.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear composition counterexample to direct proximal evaluation through a transform.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\) and \(g(u)=\lVert u\rVert_1\), the transformed function is \((g\circ A)(x)=|x_1|+2|x_2|\), hence \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda(g\circ A)}(z)=\bigl(S_\lambda(z_1),S_{2\lambda}(z_2)\bigr).\] The naive transform rule instead gives \[A^{-1}\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(Az)=\bigl(S_\lambda(z_1),\tfrac12 S_\lambda(2z_2)\bigr)=\bigl(S_\lambda(z_1),S_{\lambda/2}(z_2)\bigr).\] These expressions differ, for example whenever \(\lambda/2<|z_2|<2\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even an invertible diagonal transform can invalidate evaluation of a composite proximal map by transforming, applying the component prox, and transforming back.
knowledge_statements.title: General Transform Bottlenecks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal-transform counterexample and soft-thresholding levels are correct, and the counterexample fits the transform-bottleneck leaf. The record nevertheless lacks an inspectable source for the claimed failure of the naive transform rule.

children.title: Spectral Evaluation Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Matrix regularization dominated by large eigenvalue or singular-value computations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nuclear-norm proximal evaluation from a partial spectrum when the omitted singular values are certified below threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(\lambda>0\). Suppose singular triplets \((\sigma_i,u_i,v_i)\) are available for every \(\sigma_i>\lambda\), and it is certified that every omitted singular value is at most \(\lambda\). Then
\[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\lVert\cdot\rVert_*}(Z)=\sum_{\sigma_i>\lambda}(\sigma_i-\lambda)u_iv_i^\top.\]
Without the omitted-spectrum bound, a truncated decomposition alone does not certify exact proximal evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only singular values above the threshold contribute to the nuclear-norm proximal map, but exact truncated evaluation requires certification that no omitted singular value exceeds that threshold.
assumptions_latex: Every singular triplet with singular value greater than \(\lambda\) is computed.
Every omitted singular value is certified to be at most \(\lambda\).

notation.meaning: Singular value and associated singular vectors

knowledge_statements.title: Certified Truncated SVD Evaluation

assumptions_latex: \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is represented as a dense matrix.
Arithmetic operations are counted in the classical dense linear-algebra model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact evaluation of \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\lVert\cdot\rVert_*}(Z)\) is dominated by an SVD, with classical cost \(O(mn\min\{m,n\})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical dense cost of exact nuclear-norm proximal evaluation.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a singular value decomposition \(Z=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i)V^\top\), the nuclear-norm proximal map is \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\lVert\cdot\rVert_*}(Z)=U\operatorname{diag}\bigl((\sigma_i-\lambda)_+\bigr)V^\top.\] For a dense \(m\)-by-\(n\) matrix, computing a full exact SVD by classical dense algorithms costs \(O(mn\min\{m,n\})\) arithmetic operations and dominates the scalar thresholding cost. Consequently, exact spectral proximal evaluation can dominate each outer optimization iteration unless low-rank or partial-spectrum structure is exploitable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact nuclear-norm proximal evaluation requires singular-value decomposition, whose dense classical cost can dominate every outer iteration.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Evaluation Bottlenecks

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singular-value-thresholding formula and classical dense SVD order are standard, but the cited semidefinite-optimization section does not clearly support either the nuclear-norm proximal formula or the stated arithmetic complexity. A directly relevant locator is needed.

children.title: Nested Accuracy Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Inner component evaluation whose cost or uncertainty dominates outer optimization.

assumptions_latex: The outer update is unit-step inexact gradient descent on \(F(x)=x^2/2\).
The returned gradient at iteration \(k\) is \(x_k+e_k\), where \(e_k=\varepsilon\) for a fixed \(\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After one update, \(x_k=-\varepsilon\) for every \(k\geq1\), and the exact stationarity residual is \(\lvert F'(x_k)\rvert=\lvert\varepsilon\rvert\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent inner error creates a nonvanishing outer stationarity floor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F(x)=x^2/2\) and the inexact gradient update \[x_{k+1}=x_k-\bigl(x_k+e_k\bigr).\] If \(e_k=\varepsilon\) for a fixed \(\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\), then \(x_k=-\varepsilon\) for every \(k\geq1\), and \[\lvert F'(x_k)\rvert=\lvert\varepsilon\rvert.\] Thus a fixed nonzero inner-oracle error imposes a nonzero outer stationarity floor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A persistent inner-oracle error produces a stationarity floor equal to its absolute magnitude.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Accuracy Bottlenecks

children.title: Certificate Interpretation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on comparing or interpreting residuals, gaps, and structural certificates.

children.title: Metric-Dependent Residual Comparison
children.top_down_role: Residuals whose scales depend on steps, metrics, or reference geometries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization boundary between raw proximal displacement and the proximal-gradient mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\), define \[r_t(x)=x-\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(x-t
abla f(x)),\qquad G_t(x)=t^{-1}r_t(x).\] Then \(\|r_t(x)\|=t\|G_t(x)\|\). If \(g\equiv0\), then \(r_t(x)=t
abla f(x)\) while \(G_t(x)=
abla f(x)\). Thus a fixed tolerance on raw displacement changes its stationarity meaning with \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raw proximal displacement scales with the stepsize, whereas the normalized proximal-gradient mapping removes that scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Stepsize Scaling of Proximal Residuals

assumptions_latex: \(0<m\leq M<+\infty\), and \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite with \(mI\preceq H\preceq MI\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(r_H=x-\operatorname{prox}^{H}_{g}(x-H^{-1}\nabla f(x))\) and \(G_H=Hr_H\), one has \(\lVert G_H\rVert_{H^{-1}}=\lVert r_H\rVert_H\) and \(\sqrt m\lVert r_H\rVert_2\leq\lVert r_H\rVert_H\leq\sqrt M\lVert r_H\rVert_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization identities and spectral comparison for variable-metric proximal residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define the metric proximal map by \[\operatorname{prox}^{H}_{g}(z)=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{g(u)+\tfrac12\lVert u-z\rVert_H^2\right\}.\] At \(x\), define \[r_H=x-\operatorname{prox}^{H}_{g}\bigl(x-H^{-1}\nabla f(x)\bigr),\qquad G_H=Hr_H.\] Then \[\lVert G_H\rVert_{H^{-1}}=\lVert r_H\rVert_H\] and \[\sqrt m\lVert r_H\rVert_2\leq\lVert r_H\rVert_H\leq\sqrt M\lVert r_H\rVert_2.\] Consequently, comparisons among Euclidean, primal-metric, and dual-metric residual scales depend on the spectral bounds of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean, primal-metric, and dual-metric proximal residual scales are comparable only through the metric's spectral bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Dependent Residual Comparison

children.title: Stationarity–Objective-Quality Disconnect
children.top_down_role: Weak conversion between residual size and objective quality without additional growth structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex conversion identifying the distance factor absent from a residual-only objective-quality claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex with \(X^\star=\operatorname{argmin}F\neq\varnothing\). If \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\) and \(\partial F(x)\neq\varnothing\), then
\[0\le F(x)-\min F\le \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\operatorname{dist}(x,X^\star).\]
Consequently, if \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^\star)\le R\), then \(F(x)-\min F\le R\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex stationarity residual controls objective gap after multiplication by distance to the solution set; a uniform distance bound yields a uniform conversion.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Distance Stationarity-to-Gap Conversion

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(x=M/\varepsilon\), the stationarity residual is \(\varepsilon\) while the objective gap is \(M\).

notation.meaning: Distance from zero to the convex subdifferential

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex counterexample without a uniform growth or distance bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[F(x)=\varepsilon x+\delta_{[0,M/\varepsilon]}(x).\] This function is proper, closed, and convex, and its minimum is \(F(0)=0\). At the feasible point \(\bar x=M/\varepsilon\), \[\partial F(\bar x)=\varepsilon+[0,+\infty),\qquad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(\bar x))=\varepsilon,\] whereas \[F(\bar x)-\min F=M.\] Because \(M\) is arbitrary, a small stationarity residual alone gives no uniform bound on objective suboptimality over closed convex functions without additional bounded-distance, error-bound, or growth assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex point can have arbitrarily small stationarity residual yet arbitrarily large objective gap when no growth or distance control is assumed.
knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity–Objective-Quality Disconnect

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The endpoint subdifferential, residual, and objective gap are computed correctly, and the counterexample fits the stationarity-versus-objective-quality leaf. The record has no inspectable authoritative citation, so source support is required.

children.title: Objective-Quality–Structure-Recovery Disconnect
children.top_down_role: Near-optimal values that do not ensure support, group, rank, or face recovery.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp objective-gap condition for certifying membership in a desired structural class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F^*=\inf_xF(x)\in\mathbb R\), let \(\mathcal S\) be the set of points having the desired support, group, rank, active-face, or analogous structure, and define \[\Delta_{\mathcal S}=\inf_{x
otin\mathcal S} igl(F(x)-F^* igr).\] If \(\Delta_{\mathcal S}>0\), every \(x\) satisfying \(F(x)-F^*<\Delta_{\mathcal S}\) belongs to \(\mathcal S\). Conversely, if \(\mathcal S^c
eq\varnothing\) and \(\Delta_{\mathcal S}=0\), then for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(x
otin\mathcal S\) with \(F(x)-F^*<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective accuracy certifies a desired structure exactly when wrong-structure points are separated from the optimum by a positive objective margin.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S\) denotes the desired structural class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta_{\mathcal S}>0\Rightarrow\bigl(F(x)-F^*<\Delta_{\mathcal S}\Rightarrow x\in\mathcal S\bigr);\quad \mathcal S^c\neq\varnothing,\ \Delta_{\mathcal S}=0\Rightarrow\inf_{x\notin\mathcal S}(F(x)-F^*)=0.

notation.meaning: Set of points with the desired discrete or facial structure.
Objective separation margin from all wrong-structure points.

review_flags: reviewer_revision: required a finite optimal value so objective gaps are well-defined
knowledge_statements.title: Structural Objective-Margin Criterion

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalar lasso example separating objective accuracy from exact support recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y=\lambda+\delta\) and \(F(x)=\tfrac12(x-y)^2+\lambda|x|\) on \(\mathbb R\). Soft thresholding gives the unique minimizer \(x^\star=\delta\). The candidate \(\widehat x=0\) satisfies \[F(\widehat x)-F(x^\star)=\frac{\delta^2}{2}.\] Hence, for every objective tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), choosing \(0<\delta\leq\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\) makes \(\widehat x\) \(\varepsilon\)-optimal, although \(\operatorname{supp}(\widehat x)=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{supp}(x^\star)=\{1\}\). Thus arbitrarily accurate objective values do not alone certify recovery of support or an analogous active structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar lasso point can have an arbitrarily small objective gap while possessing the wrong support, so value accuracy alone cannot certify structural recovery.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Quality–Structure-Recovery Disconnect

children.title: Inexact-Oracle Certificate Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Reported certificates that fail to incorporate inner evaluation error.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation of simultaneous gradient-oracle and proximal-solve errors into a proximal-gradient certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(x-t\nabla f(x))\), suppose \(q\) satisfies \(\|q-\nabla f(x)\|\leq\delta\), and suppose \(z\) satisfies \[\left\|z-\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(x-tq)\right\|\leq\eta.\] Define \(G_t(x)=t^{-1}(x-p)\) and \(\widetilde G_t(x)=t^{-1}(x-z)\). Then \[\|\widetilde G_t(x)-G_t(x)\|\leq\delta+\frac{\eta}{t},\qquad \|G_t(x)\|\leq\|\widetilde G_t(x)\|+\delta+\frac{\eta}{t}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient error enters the proximal-gradient residual directly, while absolute proximal-solve error is amplified by the inverse stepsize.
assumptions_latex: The approximate proximal point has absolute error at most \(\eta\) for the inexact-gradient input.
review_flags: reviewer_revision: made differentiability at the evaluation point explicit
knowledge_statements.title: Joint Gradient-and-Proximal Oracle Error Budget

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at \(x\), and \(g:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
An inner routine returns \(z\in\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(\|z-\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(x-t\nabla f(x))\|\leq\eta\) for some \(\eta\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\widetilde G_t(x)-G_t(x)\|\leq\eta/t\), so a certificate based only on \(\|\widetilde G_t(x)\|\) omits an additive uncertainty term.

notation.meaning: Exact proximal-gradient mapping at \(x\), with \(v=x-t\nabla f(x)\).
Mapping computed from the inexact proximal point \(z\).
Absolute error of the inner proximal evaluation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional absolute proximal-evaluation error and its effect on a reported proximal-gradient residual certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v=x-t\nabla f(x)\), let \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\), and suppose an inner solver returns \(z\) satisfying \(\|z-p\|\leq\eta\). Define \(G_t(x)=t^{-1}(x-p)\) and \(\widetilde G_t(x)=t^{-1}(x-z)\). Then \[\|G_t(x)-\widetilde G_t(x)\|=t^{-1}\|z-p\|\leq\frac{\eta}{t},\qquad \|G_t(x)\|\leq\|\widetilde G_t(x)\|+\frac{\eta}{t}.\] Consequently, reporting \(\|\widetilde G_t(x)\|\leq\varepsilon\) as an \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity certificate is unjustified unless the term \(\eta/t\) is incorporated or separately controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact proximal evaluation perturbs the reported proximal-gradient mapping by at most the inner error divided by the stepsize; omitting that uncertainty can overstate stationarity.

children.title: Algorithmic Solution Procedures
children.top_down_role: Iterative solution procedures assigned to algorithm-focused chapters.

assumptions_latex: The only supplied information is a decomposition \(F=f+g\) with convex components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decomposition class alone does not specify a unique update map, stopping rule, or algorithmic output.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit alternative decompositions induce different standard updates
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite structure does not itself prescribe an algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\). With the decomposition \(f(x)=x^2\), \(g(x)=0\), a proximal-gradient step of size \(t\) is \(x^+=x-2tx\). With the equally valid decomposition \(f(x)=0\), \(g(x)=x^2\), the corresponding step is \(x^+=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(x)=x/(1+2t)\). These update maps differ for \(t>0\) and \(x\ne0\). Therefore, merely asserting convex composite form neither selects a solution procedure nor determines initialization, oracle accuracy, stopping criteria, or returned iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same convex objective admits decompositions producing different standard updates, so composite structure alone does not determine a solution procedure.
knowledge_statements.title: Algorithmic Solution Procedures

children.title: Parameter-Selection Rules
children.top_down_role: Step-size, penalty, and tuning policies assigned to algorithmic analysis.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A standard proximal-gradient stepsize restriction is \(0<t\leq1/a\), which cannot be inferred from composite form without the numerical smoothness constant \(a\).

notation.meaning: Curvature and gradient-Lipschitz constant of the smooth term.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter rules require quantitative assumptions beyond objective decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F_a(x)=f_a(x)+g(x)\), where \(f_a(x)=\tfrac a2x^2\) and \(g(x)=|x|\), the gradient of \(f_a\) is \(a\)-Lipschitz. The usual majorization condition for proximal gradient is ensured by \(0<t\leq1/a\). Because \(a\) can be any positive number while every \(F_a\) has the same qualitative smooth-plus-nonsmooth convex form, no fixed positive stepsize is justified uniformly from that form alone. Analogously, tolerances, penalty parameters, and line-search constants require numerical regularity or accuracy information not encoded by the decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composite form alone gives no valid universal stepsize: even a scalar family requires stepsizes that vary inversely with its unknown curvature.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Selection Rules

children.title: Convergence Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Convergence regimes and rate guarantees outside this structural chapter.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a proper convex composite objective with a minimizer.
No update rule or iterate condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convex composite structure alone implies no convergence of an arbitrary reported sequence.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence belongs to a specified method and assumptions, not objective syntax alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\tfrac12x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\), so \(F^\star=0\) at \(x^\star=0\). The constant sequence \(x_k=1\) for every \(k\geq0\) is compatible with knowing only that \(F\) is a convex composite objective, yet \(F(x_k)-F^\star=1/2\) and \(x_k\not\to x^\star\). Thus convergence cannot be concluded without a specified update or descent condition, admissible parameters, oracle-accuracy assumptions, and an appropriate solution-existence or level-boundedness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex composite objective does not make unspecified iterates converge; convergence requires a defined method, valid parameters, and relevant regularity assumptions.

children.title: Statistical Recovery-Selection Scope Boundary

children.title: Statistical Recovery Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Conditions for recovering parameters, signals, or structured targets.

assumptions_latex: No data-generating distribution, design condition, noise model, or parameter class is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convex regularized objective structure alone implies no uniform statistical recovery guarantee.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability and probabilistic assumptions lie beyond composite objective structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the observation be \(Y=\xi\), where the distribution of \(\xi\) is independent of an unknown parameter \(\theta\in\{-1,1\}\). The two parameter values induce identical data distributions. Consequently, for every estimator \(\widehat\theta(Y)\), at least one of the two parameters has error probability at least \(1/2\): \[\max_{\theta\in\{-1,1\}}\mathbb P_\theta\{\widehat\theta\ne\theta\}\geq\frac12.\] Expressing the estimator as a minimizer of a convex loss plus a convex regularizer cannot remove this nonidentifiability. Statistical recovery therefore requires assumptions beyond composite convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When distinct parameters generate identical data, no estimator can recover them uniformly; writing an estimator as a convex composite minimizer does not restore identifiability.
knowledge_statements.title: Statistical Recovery Guarantees

children.title: Sample-Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Sample requirements associated with statistical recovery.

assumptions_latex: The design may be degenerate and no distributional or restricted-identifiability condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite sample-size threshold depending only on composite objective form can guarantee parameter recovery.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: degenerate-design counterexample valid for every sample size
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample complexity requires a statistical model and identifiability regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(n\geq1\), take the linear model \(Y=X\beta+\xi\) with \(X=0\). Then the distribution of \(Y\) is independent of \(\beta\), regardless of sample size. In particular, minimizing a convex empirical loss plus any fixed convex regularizer cannot yield uniform recovery over two distinct admissible values \(\beta_0\ne\beta_1\). Hence no universal threshold \(n_0\) derived solely from smooth-plus-regularizer structure can ensure recovery for all \(n\geq n_0\); rates require dimension, model class, noise, design, and target-accuracy assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even infinitely many observations cannot identify a parameter under a zero design, so composite objective form alone determines no sample-complexity regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Complexity Regimes

children.title: Model-Selection Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Guarantees for identifying supports, ranks, groups, or active structures.

assumptions_latex: A linear model has two identical nonzero design columns.
The true coefficient vector is supported on exactly one of those columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact support selection is unidentifiable even when prediction is exact.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prediction equivalence does not imply exact model selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\ne0\) and \(X=[u\;u]\). For \(\beta^{(1)}=(1,0)\) and \(\beta^{(2)}=(0,1)\), one has \(X\beta^{(1)}=X\beta^{(2)}=u\), but \(\operatorname{supp}(\beta^{(1)})=\{1\}\) and \(\operatorname{supp}(\beta^{(2)})=\{2\}\). Under any observation model depending on the coefficient only through \(X\beta\), these parameters are observationally indistinguishable. Thus no estimator, including a convex regularized estimator, can uniformly guarantee exact support selection without an identifiability condition excluding such designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical design columns make two different supports observationally equivalent, so exact model selection needs design identifiability beyond convex regularization.
knowledge_statements.title: Model-Selection Guarantees

children.title: Regularization Bias Analysis
children.top_down_role: Statistical bias induced by regularization choices.

assumptions_latex: \(y=\theta\) is a noiseless scalar observation and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When \(|\theta|>\lambda\), the regularized minimizer has signed bias \(\widehat\theta-\theta=-\lambda\operatorname{sign}(\theta)\).

notation.meaning: Unknown scalar signal and noiseless observation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact shrinkage bias in the scalar quadratic-loss lasso.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\widehat\theta\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathbb R}\left\{\frac12(x-y)^2+\lambda|x|\right\},\qquad y=\theta.\] The unique solution is \(\widehat\theta=\operatorname{sign}(\theta)(|\theta|-\lambda)_+\). Hence, if \(|\theta|>\lambda\), then \(\widehat\theta-\theta=-\lambda\operatorname{sign}(\theta)\) and \(|\widehat\theta-\theta|=\lambda\); if \(|\theta|\leq\lambda\), then \(\widehat\theta=0\). This quantifies regularization bias in one model, while general bias guarantees require a specified statistical model, regularizer geometry, and parameter regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar lasso soft-thresholding shrinks every sufficiently large signal by exactly the regularization weight and sets smaller signals to zero.

children.title: Nonconvex Composite Objectives
children.top_down_role: Composite structures containing nonconvex objectives or regularizers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on transferring convex-composite conclusions to a nonconvex sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the complete proper objective \(F=f+g\) is nonconvex, conclusions requiring convexity—such as global sufficiency of convex-subdifferential stationarity, global convex subgradient inequalities, or convex-composite proximal fixed-point optimality equivalences—cannot be invoked without additional structure. Retaining a two-term decomposition does not restore those conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once the complete sum is nonconvex, convex-composite guarantees do not follow merely from retaining a two-term decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Convex-composite global conclusions are not justified solely by the decomposition }F=f+g.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Composite Guarantee Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Component Nonconvexity Does Not Determine Sum Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes componentwise nonconvexity from nonconvexity of the complete composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexity of both summands is sufficient but not necessary for convexity of their sum. For example, \(f(x)=-x^2\) and \(g(x)=2x^2\) have the convex sum \(f(x)+g(x)=x^2\), whereas \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(g(x)=-2x^2\) have the nonconvex sum \(-x^2\). Classification must therefore be applied to the complete extended-real sum, including its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex summand neither forces nor precludes a convex total objective; convexity must be checked for the complete extended-real sum.
assumptions_latex: The displayed functions are real-valued on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{convexity}(f+g)\text{ is not determined by nonconvexity of one summand alone.}
knowledge_statements.title: Component Nonconvexity Does Not Determine Sum Convexity

assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb N\), and \(f,g:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper functions such that \(F=f+g\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composite objective \(F=f+g\) is nonconvex exactly when it fails the extended-real convexity inequality for some \(x,y\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\).

notation.meaning: Effective domain of the composite objective.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard extended-real definition of nonconvexity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real finite-dimensional definition; algorithmic stationarity is not included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper composite objective \(F=f+g\) on \(\mathbb R^d\) is nonconvex if it is not convex as an extended-real-valued function. Equivalently, there exist \(x,y\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) such that \[F(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)>\alpha F(x)+(1-\alpha)F(y).\] This formulation also detects failure of convexity caused by a nonconvex effective domain, because the left-hand side may equal \(+\infty\) while the right-hand side is finite. Nonconvexity may arise from either component or from the effective-domain geometry. The representation as a sum does not itself provide global optimality certificates or justify convergence guarantees developed specifically for convex composite objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper composite objective is nonconvex when its extended-real sum violates the convexity inequality for some two ambient points and an interior convex-combination weight; this includes failure caused by a nonconvex effective domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Composite Objectives

children.title: Weakly Convex Compositions
children.top_down_role: Composite structures governed by weak convexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Nonconvexity Need Not Be Weakly Convex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of every finite global weak-convexity modulus despite smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=-x^4\) on \(\mathbb R\), every finite \(\rho\geq0\) gives \[\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\left(F(x)+\frac\rho2x^2\right)=\rho-12x^2<0\] for sufficiently large \(|x|\). Hence \(F\) is not \(\rho\)-weakly convex for any finite \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smoothness alone does not ensure global weak convexity: negative quartic curvature defeats every finite quadratic tilt.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is not }\rho\text{-weakly convex for any finite }\rho.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Nonconvexity Need Not Be Weakly Convex

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closure rules for proper sums and proper affine pullbacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If each \(F_i:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is \(\rho_i\)-weakly convex and \(\sum_iF_i\) is proper, then \(\sum_iF_i\) is \((\sum_i\rho_i)\)-weakly convex. If \(F:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex, \(A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, and \(x\mapsto F(Ax+b)\) is proper, then that pullback is \(\rho\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\)-weakly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak-convexity moduli add under proper sums and scale by the squared operator norm under proper affine pullback.
assumptions_latex: Each \(F_i\) is \(\rho_i\)-weakly convex and \(\sum_iF_i\) is proper.
\(F\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex, \(A\) is linear, and \(F(A\cdot+b)\) is proper.

notation.meaning: Euclidean operator norm of the linear map.

review_flags: reviewer_revision: added properness of the affine pullback, required by the adopted proper-function definition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard sufficient condition for weak convexity of a nonlinear composition plus a weakly convex regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable with \(\beta\)-Lipschitz Jacobian, let \(h:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz, and let \(g:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho_g\)-weakly convex. Then \[F(x)=h(c(x))+g(x)\] is \((L\beta+\rho_g)\)-weakly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex Lipschitz outer function composed with a smooth map having Lipschitz Jacobian is weakly convex; adding a weakly convex regularizer adds the moduli.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho_g\)-weakly convex.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the outer function.
Lipschitz constant of the Jacobian of the inner map.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth-Inner Lipschitz-Outer Weak-Convexity Rule

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex exactly when \(x\mapsto F(x)+\tfrac\rho2\|x\|^2\) is convex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-dimensional definition of weak convexity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean weak convexity of a possibly nonconvex composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous function \(F:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex when the tilted function \[x\longmapsto F(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\] is convex. Thus \(0\)-weak convexity is ordinary convexity, whereas \(\rho>0\) permits controlled nonconvexity. For a composition-plus-regularizer model \(F(x)=h(c(x))+g(x)\), weak convexity is an additional quantitative property to be established from assumptions on \(h\), \(c\), and \(g\); it does not follow merely from writing the objective in composite form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is rho-weakly convex when adding a quadratic of curvature rho makes it convex; composite notation alone does not establish this property.

children.title: Generalized Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Stationarity notions used beyond the convex composite setting.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of sufficiency for generalized stationarity in nonconvex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=x^3\), one has \(\partial F(0)=\{0\}\), so \(0\) is generalized stationary. Nevertheless, \(0\) is not a local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized stationary point need not be a local minimizer: zero is stationary for the cubic but is not locally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity Is Not Local Optimality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary first-order condition for an unconstrained local minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}F\) is a local minimizer, then \(0\in\widehat\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq\partial F(\bar x)\). Consequently every local minimizer is stationary in the limiting-subdifferential sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every local minimizer of a proper extended-real objective is limiting-subdifferential stationary.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.title: Limiting-Subdifferential Fermat Rule

notation.meaning: limiting (Mordukhovich) subdifferential of the extended-real-valued objective

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: limiting-subdifferential stationarity is the standard generalized first-order condition for nonsmooth nonconvex objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses limiting-subdifferential stationarity; this lies beyond purely convex composite optimality theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}F\). The point \(\bar x\) is called generalized stationary for minimizing \(F\) when
\[
0\in\partial F(\bar x),
\]
where \(\partial F(\bar x)\) is the limiting subdifferential. For a composite objective \(F=f+r\), this condition concerns the subdifferential of the complete objective; a decomposition such as \(0\in\nabla f(\bar x)+\partial r(\bar x)\) requires an applicable subdifferential sum rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible-domain point is generalized stationary when zero belongs to the limiting subdifferential of the full objective; splitting this condition across composite terms requires a valid calculus rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Stationarity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard, internally consistent, and appropriately typed as a definition, but no inspectable source supports the selected limiting-subdifferential convention or the sum-rule qualification.

children.title: Envelope-Based Analysis
children.top_down_role: Envelope constructions used for weakly convex analysis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp obstruction at and beyond the quadratic-envelope threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\rho>0\), let \(F(x)=-\tfrac{\rho}{2}\lVert x\rVert^2\). At \(\lambda=1/\rho\), the proximal subproblem is unbounded below when \(x\neq0\) and has every \(y\) as a minimizer when \(x=0\). For \(\lambda>1/\rho\), it is unbounded below for every \(x\). Thus the guarantee for \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\) cannot generally be extended to the threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reciprocal weak-convexity threshold is sharp: at or beyond it, the proximal subproblem may lose uniqueness or become unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda\geq1/\rho\ \text{does not ensure a finite single-valued proximal map or a smooth Moreau envelope.}
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Weak-Convexity Threshold

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.

notation.meaning: Moreau envelope of the objective at parameter lambda
unique proximal point of the weakly convex objective

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the Moreau-envelope gradient formula is standard for weakly convex functions below the reciprocal weak-convexity threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau-envelope analysis for finite-dimensional weakly convex objectives, outside the chapter's convex-composite core.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the Moreau envelope and proximal point by
\[
F_\lambda(x):=\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{F(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\},\qquad
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}(x):=\mathop{\arg\min}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{F(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
If \(F\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex, and if \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\), then the proximal point is unique, \(F_\lambda\) is continuously differentiable, and
\[
\nabla F_\lambda(x)=\frac{1}{\lambda}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}(x)\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Below the reciprocal weak-convexity threshold, the Moreau envelope is smooth and its gradient is the scaled displacement from a point to its unique proximal point.
knowledge_statements.title: Envelope-Based Analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weakly convex Moreau-envelope formula and threshold are precise and standard, and representation is a reasonable role for this envelope-based formula, but the differentiability, uniqueness, and gradient claims have no cited source.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Consider
\[
p^*:=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}
\]
and
\[
d^*:=\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:c-A^*y\in K^*\}.
\]
If there exists \(x^\circ\in\operatorname{int}K\) with \(Ax^\circ=b\), and \(p^*>-\infty\), then \(p^*=d^*\) and the dual supremum is attained. Thus strict primal feasibility excludes a conic duality gap under finite primal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional conic program, strict primal feasibility and finite optimal value imply zero duality gap and attainment of the dual optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Solution Theory

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Recovery Dichotomy from a Unique Lagrangian Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires strong duality, dual attainment, and uniqueness of the minimizer of the dual-optimal Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume strong duality holds for a primal problem, the dual optimum is attained at \((\lambda^*,v^*)\), and \(\mathcal L(\cdot,\lambda^*,v^*)\) has a unique minimizer \(x^*\). If \(x^*\) is primal feasible, then \(x^*\) is primal optimal. If \(x^*\) is not primal feasible, then the primal problem has no optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When strong duality and dual attainment hold, the unique minimizer of the optimal Lagrangian is the primal optimum if it is feasible; if it is infeasible, the primal optimum is not attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the primal-dual pair
\[
p^*:=\inf\left\{\langle C,X\rangle:\langle A_i,X\rangle=b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ X\succeq0\right\},
\]
\[
d^*:=\sup\left\{b^\mathsf{T}y:\sum_{i=1}^m y_iA_i+S=C,\ S\succeq0\right\}.
\]
If a matrix \(X^\circ\succ0\) satisfies all primal equalities and \(p^*>-\infty\), then \(p^*=d^*\), and there exist \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(S^*\succeq0\) attaining the dual value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equality-form semidefinite program with a positive definite feasible matrix and finite optimum has no duality gap, and its dual optimum is attained.

children.title: Facial Reduction
children.top_down_role: Facial geometry used to repair or interpret conic formulations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applicability condition for handing a nonempty conic slice to facial-reduction theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=H\cap K\neq\varnothing\), where \(H\) is affine and \(K\) is a finite-dimensional closed convex cone. Facial reduction is triggered relative to the declared cone when \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\). Equivalently, the minimal face \(F_{\min}\unlhd K\) containing \(S\) is proper. Restricting the cone to \(F_{\min}\) preserves the slice and gives \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty conic slice triggers facial reduction exactly when it has no relatively interior point in the declared cone; restriction to its minimal face restores relative strict feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite-dimensional closed convex cone.

notation.meaning: Minimal face of K containing the feasible slice.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(F_0:=K\). At iteration \(k\), stop and output \(F_k\) if \(H\cap\operatorname{ri}F_k\neq\varnothing\). Otherwise obtain a nonzero exposing vector \(z_k\in F_k^*\) satisfying \(\langle z_k,x\rangle=0\) for every \(x\in H\cap F_k\), and set
\[
F_{k+1}:=F_k\cap z_k^\perp.
\]
Each nonterminal step produces a proper face containing \(H\cap K\). In finite dimensions the process terminates after finitely many strict face reductions at a face \(F_t\) such that \(H\cap K=H\cap F_t\) and \(H\cap\operatorname{ri}F_t\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly intersect the cone with exposing hyperplanes that preserve feasibility. The process reaches a smaller face on which the constraints become relatively strictly feasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given strictly feasible \((x_0,y_0,s_0)\) for \(Ax=b\), \(A^*y+s=c\), \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\), and \(s\in\operatorname{int}K^*\), choose \(\mu_0>0\). At iteration \(k\), form the Newton linearization of primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and the barrier centrality equation
\[
s+\mu_k\nabla\Phi(x)=0.
\]
Compute a direction \((\Delta x_k,\Delta y_k,\Delta s_k)\), choose \(\alpha_k>0\) preserving strict cone membership, update
\[
(x_{k+1},y_{k+1},s_{k+1})=(x_k,y_k,s_k)+\alpha_k(\Delta x_k,\Delta y_k,\Delta s_k),
\]
and decrease \(\mu_k\). Stop when feasibility residuals and the primal-dual gap meet their prescribed tolerances; output the final iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-dual interior-point method follows barrier centrality equations with Newton steps, preserves strict cone feasibility, decreases the barrier parameter, and stops at specified residual and gap tolerances.
